Review Assumptions

Domain of the expert reviewer

Applied Strategic R&D Programme Management, with expertise in electrochemistry, materials science commercialization, and technology-invention risk across capital-constrained, non-commercial research environments. Focus on translating laboratory breakthroughs to demonstrated prototypes and defensible IP while managing scientific, operational, and financial risk over multi-year timelines.

Domain-specific considerations

  • Chemistry-to-cell translation penalties: material-level energy density often collapses 15–30% once packaging, current collectors, electrolyte mass and pressure hardware are included; volumetric density constraints are especially harsh and often treated as secondary
  • Cycle-life and degradation mechanisms: high-energy lithium-rich cells commonly sacrifice cycle life; a 500 Wh/kg cell with <200 cycles is not a functional battery, yet the plan lacks a non-negotiable minimum threshold until Month 6 (2027-04-14)
  • Interface engineering risk: solid electrolytes, high-voltage cathodes and lithium-metal anodes all depend critically on stable interphase chemistry that is often discovered only after hundreds of test cells; early forensics access is essential
  • Permitting and site readiness: hazardous-materials synthesis and thermal-runaway testing in the Austin area face multi-agency approvals (EPA, TCEQ, local fire authority); a 6–8 month delay is plausible and compresses the effective 84-month timeline
  • Talent concentration and IP contamination: proximity to Tesla creates both advantage (recruitment) and risk (poaching, implicit knowledge transfer); clean-room protocols and retention mechanics need explicit design
  • Pilot-line capital lock-in: a new dry-room and pouch-cell line costs USD 30–60 M and requires 6–12 months to commission; committing that capital before a winning chemistry is proven is a major bet, but leasing adds queue time and confidentiality exposure

Issue 1 - Missing Explicit Minimum Cycle-Life Requirement and Late-Discovery Risk

The plan states 500 Wh/kg and 1000 Wh/L targets but does not define a minimum cycle-life threshold (e.g., ≥300 cycles at 80% capacity retention) until Month 6 (2027-04-14), and even then only as a proposal. A cell meeting the gravimetric and volumetric targets but cycling <150 times would satisfy the letter of the success criteria while being commercially unusable. This absence creates the risk of a 'one-cycle wonder' that wastes 12–18 months of development before cycle-life inadequacy is discovered.

Recommendation: Establish a hard minimum cycle-life requirement by Month 3 (2027-01-14) as a non-negotiable gate criterion: propose ≥300 cycles at 80% capacity retention at the pouch-cell level. Include cycle-life data collection and degradation-mechanism forensics (post-mortem SEMs of cycled electrodes, electrolyte decomposition analysis) from Month 6 (2027-04-14) onward for every candidate chemistry. Require every chemistry finalist advancing past Month 24 (2028-10-14) to demonstrate measured cycle-life evidence, not projections. If a leading candidate fails this threshold by Month 30 (2029-04-14), demote it immediately and accelerate the reserve chemistry into testing.

Sensitivity: Baseline assumption: a viable chemistry is discovered by Month 30 (2029-04-14) with ≥300 cycles. If cycle-life is discovered to be inadequate only at Month 48 (2030-10-14) (late discovery), a redesign cycle or chemistry pivot would cost USD 10–25 M and delay delivery by 6–12 months. Late-discovered cycle-life issues would also reduce the programme's credibility and patent value by an estimated 20–30%, as a documented poor-cycle-life result is harder to license and commercialize than early-caught and remedied limitations.

Issue 2 - Volumetric Energy Density (1000 Wh/L) Secondary Treatment and Cell-Architecture Risk

The strategy emphasizes gravimetric density (500 Wh/kg) in chemistry and discovery choices, yet volumetric density (1000 Wh/L) is equally challenging and depends on thin separators, low dead-volume architectures, and high-density cathode structures. Lithium-sulfur and conversion-cathode chemistries can hit Wh/kg but often require thick electrolyte layers or low-density materials that erode Wh/L. The plan's dual-track mass-and-volume model is a good safeguard, but the model is not verified experimentally until Month 30 (2029-04-14), risking 18 months of wasted effort on a chemistry that fundamentally cannot achieve 1000 Wh/L at cell level.

Recommendation: Elevate volumetric density to parity with gravimetric density from Month 12 (2027-10-14) onward. Require the live mass-and-volume model to project Wh/L alongside Wh/kg for every candidate; flag any chemistry projecting <950 Wh/L at pouch level by Month 18 (2028-04-14) for immediate redesign (bipolar stacking, anode-free optimization, or aggressive separator thinning). Mandate independent third-party measured pouch-cell data showing both ≥500 Wh/kg and ≥950 Wh/L in the same cells by Month 30 (2029-04-14), not separate demonstrations. If a chemistry hits the Wh/kg target but falls short of 950 Wh/L by Month 36 (2029-10-14), allocate a focused 6-month architecture sprint before the mid-gate decision rather than deferring volumetric work to later phases.

Sensitivity: Baseline: a winning chemistry achieves both 500 Wh/kg and 1000 Wh/L by Month 36 (2029-10-14). Downside scenario: if volumetric penalties (thick separators, large electrolyte volume) limit a leading chemistry to 850 Wh/L despite 520 Wh/kg, and this is discovered at Month 36 (2029-10-14), a 6–12 month redesign cycle consuming USD 8–15 M would compress the final optimization window. Worst case (late discovery at Month 60 = 2031-10-14): the programme would deliver a partial success (500 Wh/kg but only 800 Wh/L), missing one of two co-equal targets and reducing the invention's value by an estimated 30–40% as a licensing asset.

Issue 3 - Site Permitting, Regulatory Approval and Operational-Readiness Schedule Compression

The plan assumes site selection, lease negotiation and permitting can be completed by Month 3 (2027-01-14), allowing pilot-line deployment by Months 3–6 (2027-01-14 to 2027-04-14). In practice, EPA hazardous-waste permits, TCEQ air and water permits, and Austin Fire Authority approvals for lithium-metal synthesis and thermal-runaway abuse testing typically require 4–8 months, especially if the site is new to such materials. A permitting delay of 6–8 months (plausible and common in R&D facilities) would push operational start to Month 6–8 (2027-04-14 to 2027-06-14), compressing the 84-month timeline to 76–78 months of effective work. Conservative permitting also risks excluding reactive chemistries (lithium metal, sulfides, halide electrolytes) from on-site synthesis, forcing outsourcing of key chemistry work at cost and with 4–6 week turnarounds, slowing iteration 50–70%.

Recommendation: Initiate site selection, lease negotiation and permitting engagement with Texas environmental and Austin fire authorities in Month 0 (2026-10-14), not Month 1 (2026-11-14). Treat regulators as collaborative partners, not gatekeepers; propose a tiered permitting strategy with the fire authority: Phase 1 (dry-room and pouch-cell assembly, low-hazard) by Month 3 (2027-01-14), Phase 2 (lithium-metal and solvent synthesis) by Month 6 (2027-04-14), Phase 3 (abuse-testing chambers) by Month 9 (2027-07-14). Pre-negotiate with licensed external synthesis facilities (e.g., contract research organizations in Texas or California) to handle any on-site-prohibited chemistry steps at cost-plus terms with <4 week turnarounds, so synthesis is not a bottleneck if local permitting is restrictive. By Month 1 (2026-11-14), establish an EHS compliance function led by an experienced battery-lab engineer who can navigate overlapping EPA, TCEQ and local rules.

Sensitivity: Baseline: operational start by Month 3 (2027-01-14); effective programme work spans Months 3–84 (2027-01-14 to 2033-10-14) = 81 months. Downside scenario (6-month permitting delay): operational start at Month 9 (2027-07-14), effective work = 75 months. Impact on timeline: with a Month 36 (2029-10-14) chemistry gate, a 6-month delay compresses the post-gate window from 48 months to 42 months. A chemistry pivot triggered at the gate would then have only ~36 months to maturation and proof—risking incomplete validation. Cost impact: outsourced synthesis of lithium-metal and sulfide candidate batches at USD 50–100 K per batch could consume USD 2–5 M/year if on-site synthesis is prohibited, reducing remaining capital budget by 5–12%.

Issue 4 - Pilot-Line Capital Commitment Before Chemistry is Proven: Ownership Versus Leasing Trade-Off

The plan specifies a modular, containerized dry-room and pouch-cell line sized for 50–100 cells/month but does not explicitly decide whether to build (~USD 30–50 M, 6–12 month lead time), lease (~USD 2–5 M/year operational cost, 4–8 week queue times), or modularize (~USD 15–25 M, 3–4 month deployment). Building a line early (Month 0–3 = 2026-10-14 to 2027-01-14) locks USD 30–50 M of the fixed USD 300 M budget before a winning chemistry is known, leaving USD 250–270 M for 6.5 years of operation. Leasing preserves capital for pivots but adds queue time and confidentiality exposure for unpublished materials. A new-build line also creates stranded-asset risk if the winning chemistry requires fundamentally different dry-room conditions (e.g., inert atmosphere versus moisture control) than initially assumed.

Recommendation: By Month 1 (2026-11-14), commit to a modular, leased dry-room and pouch-cell line (not owned) to preserve capital flexibility and pivot capacity. Target deployment by Month 3 (2027-01-14); negotiate a 3-year lease with expansion and early-exit options. Simultaneously, negotiate a standby pilot-line agreement with a university or national-laboratory partner by Month 2 (2026-12-14) to provide backup pouch-cell fabrication at cost during modular-line commissioning or if primary line capacity is exceeded. This converts a large fixed cost (owned line) into a variable, scalable cost (leased line). Reserve USD 15–20 M and 6-month lead time in the budget for pilot-line capital needs. If a winning chemistry by Month 24 (2028-10-14) emerges with high-throughput demands (e.g., parallel screening of 200+ cells/month), then evaluate building a dedicated line at that point with concrete chemistry-driven specifications.

Sensitivity: Baseline: modular leased line, ~USD 50–100 K/month operational cost, ~USD 0.6–1.2 M/year. Downside scenario (owned line): USD 40 M upfront commitment at Month 3 (2027-01-14), reducing available working capital by 13% and increasing sunk-cost risk. If the winning chemistry (discovered Month 36 = 2029-10-14) has dry-room requirements not met by the built line (e.g., aggressive lithium-metal work requires <10 ppm water, existing line cannot achieve), a redesign of the owned line could cost USD 5–10 M and lose 3–4 months to retrofit. Benefit of leasing: if a pivot is needed at Month 36 (2029-10-14), switching line vendors takes 2–4 weeks instead of 6–12 months for owned-line recommissioning.

Issue 5 - Chemistry-Tournament Contingency Planning and Mid-Gate Pivot Cost

The Pragmatic Foundation strategy runs a staged tournament across three or four chemistries with a formal go/no-go gate at Month 36 (2029-10-14). If two of the three leading candidates fail by Month 36 (2029-10-14) for fundamental reasons (cycle-life collapse, dendrite growth, volume expansion), the programme must pivot to a reserve chemistry with only 48 months remaining. However, pivoting from one chemistry to another (e.g., lithium-sulfur to anode-free solid-state) requires 6–10 months of precursor re-sourcing, pilot-line retooling, and staff retraining. The plan assumes pivots are 'clean,' but in practice a pivot discovered at Month 36 (2029-10-14) might not complete chemistry commissioning until Month 42–46 (2030-04-14 to 2030-08-14), leaving only 38–42 months for proof and optimization—insufficient for a chemistry reaching its first stable pouch cells.

Recommendation: By Month 12 (2027-10-14), develop detailed contingency plans for each reserve chemistry: pre-qualify precursor suppliers, document process variations and equipment reconfiguration needs, and cross-train 20–30% of the synthesis and pilot-line team on each backup path. Establish a 'pivot runway' contingency reserve of USD 10–15 M (3–5% of total budget) held unallocated through Month 30 (2029-04-14), earmarked for rapid chemistry pivots. By Month 24 (2028-10-14), if two of the three leading candidates show fundamental limitations (e.g., both stuck below 250 cycles despite 18 months of interface engineering), pre-stage the third chemistry: order long-lead precursors, prepare pilot-line equipment and train staff. This shortens the pivot execution time from 6–10 months to 4–6 weeks, allowing a Month 30–36 (2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14) decision to translate into Month 36–42 (2029-10-14 to 2030-04-14) commissioning of the pivoted chemistry, preserving 42 months for proof.

Sensitivity: Baseline: successful chemistry identified by Month 30 (2029-04-14), no pivot needed. Downside scenario (pivot at Month 36 = 2029-10-14): if pivot requires 6–10 months of retooling and commissioning, the programme reaches Month 42–46 (2030-04-14 to 2030-08-14) before the new chemistry is building pouch cells. With only 38–42 months remaining, proof-of-concept (Wh/kg and Wh/L) might be achieved but with insufficient time for reliability testing (500+ cycles, abuse tests, third-party verification). Cost of late pivot: USD 5–10 M in retooling, precursor qualification and staff retraining, reducing working capital by 1.7–3.3%. Worst case (no contingency plan): a pivot at Month 36 (2029-10-14) with unprepared suppliers and untrained staff could stretch to Month 50+, leaving only 34 months for final proof, risking an incomplete demonstration.

Issue 6 - Talent Recruitment, Retention and Payroll Budget Allocation Under Tesla Competition

The plan assumes 80–120 FTE (estimate) with payroll of USD 8–12 M/year, approximately 19–28% of the average annual budget. However, this estimate lacks detail on salary competitiveness, sign-on incentives, retention mechanics and graduate-student cost scaling. In the Austin area, senior battery scientists and manufacturing engineers earn USD 150–250 K/year in industry (Tesla, other EV firms), compared to USD 120–180 K in academic or research settings. To recruit and retain specialized talent while remaining within 25% of annual budget requires either: (a) offering industry-competitive salaries (pushing payroll toward the upper 28% estimate) and accepting reduced capital spending on equipment, or (b) offsetting lower base salaries with graduate-student pipelines, publication prestige, and retention agreements—all requiring active management. Unmanaged, payroll could exceed budget and attrition could reach 20% annually, requiring continuous re-hiring and knowledge loss.

Recommendation: Structure compensation to compete with local industry: pay a 15–20% premium over baseline academic salaries for senior chemistry and engineering leads (estimated incremental cost: USD 1–2 M/year across 5–8 key roles). Augment with signing bonuses (USD 50–150 K for mid-career scientists) and professional-development budgets (USD 10–20 K/person/year). For cost control, target 20–30% of the team as postdoctoral and graduate-student roles, reducing average payroll cost. By Month 2 (2026-12-14), negotiate a formal recruitment pipeline with University of Texas at Austin graduate and postdoctoral groups, offering stipend supplements and co-authorship on publications. Establish 3–5 year retention agreements with key personnel (chemistry leads, characterization experts) that include clawback terms for early departure. Implement a 'stay' plan: publish early wins (Month 6–12 = 2027-04-14 to 2027-10-14) in peer-reviewed journals to enhance researcher prestige and reduce poaching risk. Target attrition below 15% (proposed); if actual attrition exceeds 15%, trigger a retention review and compensation adjustment by Month 24 (2028-10-14).

Sensitivity: Baseline: average payroll USD 10 M/year (25% of annual budget), attrition <15%, turnover cost ~USD 1–2 M/year. Downside scenario (high attrition): if attrition reaches 20%, the programme must hire 16–24 replacements annually, consuming USD 1.5–2.5 M/year in recruiting, onboarding, and training (~3 months ramp-up per new hire). Loss of a key chemistry lead at Month 12–24 (2027-10-14 to 2028-10-14) could set the programme back 2–4 months as knowledge and tribal understanding is re-built. Salary-competition pressure: if competing firms raise offers by 20% (plausible in a tight Austin market), the programme would need USD 1–2 M incremental annually to retain competitiveness, compressing equipment or partner budgets by 2–5%.

Issue 7 - Characterization and Forensics Access: Partner Dependency and Queue-Time Risk

The Pragmatic Foundation strategy relies on university and national-laboratory partnerships for operando and post-mortem characterization (X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) to keep in-house instrument costs low. However, academic facilities have competing priorities, shifting schedules and occasional closures or staff departures. A 4–8 week queue at a partner facility would slow the design-build-test loop from 1–2 weeks (in-house) to 6–10 weeks, reducing the number of testable hypotheses per year by 50–75%. If a critical partner facility becomes unavailable (renovation, competing project priority, staff turnover), characterization would be outsourced to commercial labs at USD 50–100 K per failed cell, quickly exhausting a characterization budget.

Recommendation: Negotiate formal standing agreements with at least two university or national-laboratory characterization facilities by Month 3 (2027-01-14), specifying guaranteed access, turnaround (proposed: ≤3 weeks) and annual cost-sharing commitments (proposed: ≥15% of shared materials and characterization costs borne by partners). Invest in one core in-house post-mortem instrument (scanning electron microscope or X-ray diffraction: USD 2–3 M) by Month 6 (2027-04-14) for rapid triage of failed cells; outsource deeper operando work (operando XRD, in situ TEM) to partners with specialized equipment. Establish a forensics protocol by Month 3 (2027-01-14): every failed cell receives a standardized autopsy within one week of failure, with a structured root-cause report that feeds directly into the next design iteration. Develop a 'forensics atlas' (internal database of failure modes, their mechanisms and design consequences) by Month 12 (2027-10-14), so patterns across multiple cells can be identified and mitigated. Budget USD 2–3 M/year for commercial characterization services as a backstop if partner access is lost.

Sensitivity: Baseline: partner access with ≤3 week turnarounds, in-house triage capability, cost-sharing covered by partners. Downside scenario (loss of primary partner): if a key partner facility becomes unavailable at Month 18 (2028-04-14), outsourcing characterization at USD 80 K/cell for 50 cells/year would cost USD 4 M/year vs. ~USD 1.5 M with partner access, consuming USD 2.5 M/year additional budget (~6% of annual spend). Secondary scenario (queue delays): if partner queues extend to 6–8 weeks, the discovery loop slows to 1 hypothesis per 2 months instead of per 2 weeks, reducing annual hypothesis throughput by 50% and delaying identification of viable candidates by 3–6 months.

Review conclusion

This battery-invention programme targets a 500 Wh/kg, 1000 Wh/L cell within a fixed USD 300 M, 7-year timeline through a staged chemistry tournament and risk-hedged operations. The Pragmatic Foundation strategy is sound in its emphasis on hedging chemistry risk with a formal gate and on imposing system-level (mass-and-volume) discipline early. However, five critical gaps emerge: (1) minimum cycle-life is undefined as a hard threshold until Month 6 (2027-04-14), risking months of wasted effort on non-functional cells; (2) volumetric density (1000 Wh/L) is subordinate to gravimetric density in discovery priorities, yet emerging as equally challenging; (3) site permitting and regulatory readiness are assumed complete by Month 3 (2027-01-14), but 6–8 month delays are plausible and would compress effective work time 5–10%; (4) the pilot-line ownership-versus-leasing decision is unresolved, risking either USD 30–50 M of sunk capital before chemistry is proven or prolonged queue times that slow discovery 50%; and (5) talent recruitment and retention rely on untested compensation models in a competitive Austin market and assume <15% attrition without concrete mechanics. The programme should: establish cycle-life and volumetric-density thresholds by Month 3 (2027-01-14); prioritize site permitting engagement in Month 0 (2026-10-14); commit to leased (not owned) pilot-line capacity by Month 1 (2026-11-14); pre-stage reserve chemistry contingencies by Month 24 (2028-10-14); and detail compensation, partnership agreements and governance by Month 2 (2026-12-14). The fixed USD 300 M budget is adequate only if early capital commitments (facility, pilot line, hiring) are controlled, permits are secured without major delays, and partner relationships provide cost-sharing and instrument access. A 20–30% overrun in any single area (permitting delays, pilot-line build, partner loss) would compress working capital by 5–15%, risking incomplete final validation or forced descent to a lower-ambition result (e.g., 480 Wh/kg instead of 500, or skipped abuse testing).

Governance Audit

Audit - Corruption Risks

  • Bribery or kickbacks in supplier selection for expensive precursor materials (lithium compounds, fluorinated solvents) or characterization equipment, particularly with competing vendors bidding for long-term contracts (Months 3–12 = 2027-01-14 to 2027-10-14 and ongoing).
  • Nepotism or favoritism in hiring 80–120 FTE positions, especially senior chemistry and characterization leads, given the concentrated Austin battery talent pool and recruitment pressure near Tesla.
  • Conflicts of interest: employees hired from Tesla or competing firms retain undisclosed knowledge of competitor work or supplier relationships, creating steering toward favored vendors or confidential information misuse.
  • IP theft or unauthorized disclosure: programme members publish or patent pre-competitive findings via partner agreements without proper review gates, undermining patentability or licensing value.
  • Kickbacks masked as inflated 'partner co-funding' contributions: universities or national laboratories claim cost-sharing (proposed ≥15% of shared costs) but provide below-value services or inflate hours/materials costs.
  • Trading favors with regulators: selective compliance with Austin Fire Authority or TCEQ permitting, or delayed enforcement for favored research in exchange for regulatory officer involvement in publications or advisory roles.

Audit - Misallocation Risks

  • Budget misuse: front-loaded capital spending on pilot-line equipment (USD 30–50 M estimate), dry-room build and characterization instruments before chemistry is proven, consuming reserves needed for pivots or late-stage optimization.
  • Double-spending or cost-shadowing: overlapping payments to external contractors and in-house teams for duplicate synthesis, characterization or data-analysis work without documented handoff or deduplication review.
  • Inefficient precursor procurement: failing to negotiate dual-sourced suppliers by Month 3 (2027-01-14), resulting in single-vendor lock-in, price inflation (proposed risk: 20–30% above market) and USD 2–5 M/year waste.
  • Misallocated staff effort: postdoctoral and graduate students (20–30% of team) assigned to routine maintenance or administrative tasks instead of high-impact discovery work, reducing hypothesis throughput by 20–30%.
  • Scope creep and untracked experiment budgets: laboratory groups pursuing secondary chemistries or cell formats not formally gated or funded, consuming reagents, equipment time and staff capacity without visibility to the Steering Committee.
  • Undocumented outsourced synthesis or testing: if permitting delays force external contracting (estimated USD 2–5 M/year), cost-plus pricing or invoice disputes could inflate apparent costs by 15–25% without competitive bidding records.

Audit - Procedures

  • Quarterly financial and progress audits (Months 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-14, 2027-04-14, 2027-07-14, 2027-10-14, …, 84): review monthly spend by category (payroll, capital, consumables, partner, testing) against tranches and budget allocation (estimated USD 70 M payroll, USD 50 M capital, USD 25 M facility, USD 135 M variable); verify no line exceeds ±15% of plan without Steering Committee approval and document reallocations.
  • Supplier and contract audit (Months 0, 6, 18, 30, 42, 60 = 2026-10-14, 2027-04-14, 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2030-04-14, 2031-10-14): verify dual-sourced or three-sourced competitive bids for all precursors with >USD 100 K annual spend and all capital equipment >USD 1 M; confirm pricing consistency with market benchmarks and no single-vendor lock-in; reconcile invoices to purchase orders and received quantity.
  • Payroll and staffing audit (Months 3, 9, 18, 30, 48, 72 = 2027-01-14, 2027-07-14, 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2030-10-14, 2032-10-14): verify 80–120 FTE headcount accuracy, salary conformity with approved compensation bands (+15–20% premium for senior roles, proposed), on-time payment of sign-on bonuses and retention agreements; track attrition rate and replacement cost against the <15% target (proposed).
  • IP and publication compliance audit (Months 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72 = 2027-04-14, 2027-10-14, 2028-10-14, 2029-10-14, 2030-10-14, 2031-10-14, 2032-10-14): review all internal technical reports, conference presentations and patent applications before release to verify compliance with 6-month partner review windows (proposed) and clean-room onboarding protocols for Tesla-hired staff; confirm no unpermitted disclosure of pre-competitive findings.
  • Gate and technical-data audit (Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14): independent red team (2–3 scientists, external to core) replicates a sample (≥1) of cell-build and cycling data reported by each chemistry team before gate decision; confirm cell-level mass-and-volume model methodology and verify no inflated Wh/kg claims from material-level artifacts.
  • Partner cost-sharing and deliverable audit (Months 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72 = 2027-10-14, 2028-10-14, 2029-10-14, 2030-10-14, 2031-10-14, 2032-10-14): reconcile partner invoices and in-kind contributions (≥15% of shared costs proposed) to formal agreements; verify characterization turnaround (≤3 weeks proposed) and data quality; confirm backup partner capacity agreements are in place and tested by Month 6 (2027-04-14).
  • EHS compliance and permitting audit (Months 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 24, 36 = 2026-11-14, 2027-01-14, 2027-04-14, 2027-07-14, 2027-10-14, 2028-10-14, 2029-10-14): verify Phase 1–3 permits obtained on schedule; confirm hazardous-materials inventory, waste handling and incident reporting per EPA, OSHA and TCEQ; document quarterly internal EHS audits and confirm no serious incidents; validate regulatory-monitoring consulting retainer is active.

Audit - Transparency Measures

  • Monthly Steering Committee financial dashboard: published summary (internal to funder and Steering Committee) of cumulative spend by budget category, remaining tranches and reserve allocation, variance from plan by ±15% threshold, and any pending reallocations requiring approval; refreshed within 10 days of month-end.
  • Quarterly technical-progress report (Months 3, 6, 9 = 2027-01-14, 2027-04-14, 2027-07-14, …, 84): documented summary by chemistry team of cell builds, cycling data, Wh/kg and Wh/L measurements against the cell-level mass-and-volume model, cycle-life and safety thresholds (proposed ≥300 cycles at 80%, thermal runaway ≥120°C), with Steering Committee review; red-team replication results included at gates.
  • Gate-decision documentation (Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14): published to funder and Steering Committee go/no-go criteria applied (Month 18 = 2028-04-14 projected cell-level ≥500 Wh/kg and ≥950 Wh/L; Month 30 = 2029-04-14 measured pouch-cell proof with ≥3 replicates; Month 36 = 2029-10-14 selection of finalist meeting all thresholds), decision rationale, and forward-plan if contingency paths activated.
  • Supplier and contract register: maintained and shared with funder and governance committee; lists all vendors >USD 100 K spend (precursors, equipment, testing), contract terms, pricing benchmarks, sole-source justifications and competitive-bid documentation (or escalation approvals if sole-source is necessary).
  • IP filing and publication log: published schedule of patent applications (provisional and utility), research publications and technology-transfer disclosures, with filing dates, inventor teams and review compliance status; confirms 6-month partner-review windows (proposed) and clean-room onboarding attestations.
  • Staffing and retention dashboard: quarterly report to Steering Committee of headcount by role (senior, postdoctoral, graduate), attrition rate (measured; target <15%, proposed), new hires and departures with reason codes, and salary-band conformity; escalates >15% attrition for compensation review by Month 24 (2028-10-14).
  • Regulatory and EHS public summary: annual statement submitted to Austin Fire Authority, TCEQ and funder describing permits held (Phase 1–3), incident history (none expected; zero reportable incidents is the target), waste-stream volumes and disposal routes, and compliance audit results; establishes community transparency and regulator confidence.

Internal Governance Bodies

1. Scientific Steering Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: Manages strategic direction, gate decisions (Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14) and major resource allocation in a high-ambition, capital-constrained R&D programme with three competing chemistry pathways. Resolves disputes over chemistry advancement, budget reallocation and pivot decisions. Ensures evidence-linked tranche release and protects programme credibility through independent oversight of claims.

Responsibilities:

  • Approve chemistry-tournament structure and success criteria by Month 3 (2027-01-14); decide funding allocation among active teams
  • Conduct Month 18, 30 and 36 (2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14) gate reviews, applying documented go/no-go criteria and independent red-team verification results
  • Authorize chemistry selection at Month 36 (2029-10-14); approve reserve activation and major pivots if needed
  • Approve tranche releases (T2 at Month 12 = 2027-10-14, T3 at Month 24 = 2028-10-14, T4 at Month 36 = 2029-10-14) linked to milestones; manage USD 20M reserve and pivot-runway allocation
  • Oversee risk management: review technical risks (chemistry, volumetric density, cycle-life, safety), operational risks (permitting delays, talent attrition, partner dependency) and financial risks (budget burn, cost overruns) quarterly
  • Review and approve IP strategy by Month 2 (2026-12-14), licensing framework by Month 24 (2028-10-14) and commercialization plan by Month 72 (2032-10-14)

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish Committee membership (director, four chemistry leads, external technical advisor, funder representative) by Month 1 (2026-11-14)
  • Document decision authority: financial thresholds (Steering Committee authorizes decisions >USD 2M or >20% of annual tranche; Director authorizes USD 500K-2M within approved budget), escalation path (funder for programme stop or major descope), and conflict resolution (majority vote with tie-breaker by Director)
  • Set Committee meeting cadence: monthly (first 12 months) then quarterly, with 3-week gate-review cycles at Months 18, 30, 36 (2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14)
  • Define gate criteria and success metrics by Month 3 (2027-01-14): Month 18 (2028-04-14) = projected cell-level ≥500 Wh/kg and ≥950 Wh/L plus cycle-life data; Month 30 (2029-04-14) = measured pouch cells meeting thresholds; Month 36 (2029-10-14) = one finalist selected
  • Appoint independent red team (2-3 external or in-house non-core scientists) by Month 1 (2026-11-14) reporting directly to Steering Committee
  • Establish decision documentation protocol: gate decisions, financial approvals, and risk escalations recorded and shared with funder within 5 days

Membership:

  • Programme Director (chair)
  • Senior Chemistry Lead (lithium-sulfur pathway, e.g.)
  • Senior Chemistry Lead (anode-free solid-state pathway, e.g.)
  • Senior Chemistry Lead (conversion cathode or reserve pathway, e.g.)
  • Chief Technology Officer or Deputy Director (operational oversight liaison)
  • External Technical Advisor (independent expert from battery research community)
  • Funder Representative (non-voting observer, approves releases and stop decisions)

Decision Rights: Steering Committee holds exclusive authority over chemistry tournament structure and finalist selection (Month 36 = 2029-10-14), tranche release (T2-T4) conditioned on milestones, reserve allocation and programme pivots costing >USD 5M. Director (chair) has delegated authority to approve decisions up to USD 2M within approved tranches and to reallocate within 15% of chemistry-team budgets. Funder representative approves any decision to stop or descope the programme. Red team has authority to challenge progress claims and delay gate decisions up to 3 weeks for independent verification.

Decision Mechanism: Majority vote among Committee members (7 members; 4 required for quorum). Tie-breaker: Director casts second vote if tie occurs. Red team replication results (pass/fail on key claims) are required inputs to Month 18, 30 and 36 (2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14) gates and must be presented in writing ≥5 days before gate meeting. If red team flags unresolved inconsistencies, gate decision deferred ≤3 weeks for remedial verification; if unresolved after 3 weeks, gate advances but flag is escalated to funder. Financial decisions >USD 5M require unanimous consent or funder sign-off.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly full meetings Months 0-12 (2026-10-14 to 2027-10-14), then quarterly Months 12-84 (2027-10-14 to 2033-10-14). Emergency meetings ≤48 hours if a critical risk surfaces (e.g., major chemistry failure, permitting denial, partner loss). Gate review cycles at Months 18, 30, 36 (2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14) conducted over 3 weeks: Week 1 red-team verification report, Week 2 chemistry-team response and Steering Committee deliberation, Week 3 final decision and communication to funder.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Progress reports from each chemistry team: cell builds, cycling data, measured Wh/kg and Wh/L, cycle-life performance, safety-test results, comparison to cell-level mass-and-volume model
  • Risk register review: technical (chemistry, volumetric density, cycle-life, safety), operational (permitting, talent, partner access, supply chain), financial (burn rate, cost overruns, currency exposure); escalation of any risk approaching trigger thresholds
  • Red-team findings: replication results, challenged claims, unresolved discrepancies and remedial actions
  • Financial dashboard: cumulative spend by category, remaining tranches, reserve utilization, variance from plan, pending reallocations
  • Partnership and characterization access status: partner deliverables, queue times, backup-partner activation if needed
  • IP and regulatory updates: patent applications filed, publications reviewed for compliance, permit status, EHS incidents and corrective actions

Escalation Path: Steering Committee escalates to the Funder (non-voting member) any decision involving: (i) programme stop or >25% descope, (ii) additional funding beyond USD 300M cap, (iii) major chemistry-path change deviating from tournament structure (e.g., adding a fourth active chemistry or abandoning one before Month 30 = 2029-04-14), (iv) financial overrun >20% of current tranche. Red team escalates directly to Steering Committee (bypassing chemistry leads) any unresolved claim inconsistency or high-risk safety issue. Steering Committee escalates to Funder within 48 hours any incident threatening permitting, safety or regulatory compliance.

2. Chemistry and Discovery Leadership Team

Rationale for Inclusion: Manages day-to-day R&D execution across three active chemistry pathways plus reserve. Owns synthesis, pouch-cell fabrication, electrochemical characterization, failure analysis and iteration pace. Reports progress, cycle-life data and safety results to Steering Committee; escalates risks and resource conflicts. Team structure hedges chemistry risk while maintaining focus and preventing runaway scope.

Responsibilities:

  • Execute chemistry-tournament strategy: maintain three active teams (lithium-sulfur, anode-free solid-state, conversion cathode or similar) with clear leads and budgets; manage weekly team meetings, monthly progress reviews and adherence to gate criteria
  • Design, build and cycle cells: execute pouch-cell fabrication (50-100 cells/month by Month 24 = 2028-10-14), manage pilot-line scheduling, document build parameters and correlate cell performance to process variables
  • Measure energy density and cycle life: characterize all cells for Wh/kg, Wh/L, cycle retention at defined rates and temperatures; report data against cell-level mass-and-volume model within one week of completion
  • Manage failure forensics: autopsy every failed cell within one week using standardized protocol; perform post-mortem microscopy, electrolyte analysis and impedance testing; populate forensics atlas with root causes and design-change implications
  • Oversee characterization scheduling: coordinate with university and national-lab partners for operando and post-mortem analysis; manage backlogs and escalate queue delays >3 weeks to Steering Committee
  • Track safety and abuse testing: schedule thermal-ramp screening and contracted abuse tests per phased plan; maintain thermal-runaway thresholds (proposed: ≥120°C for finalists); escalate any chemistry dropping below safety thresholds to red team for gate impact

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Define chemistry-team leads and core members by Month 1 (2026-11-14); allocate budget per team proportional to strategic priority (proposed: equal initial share, rebalanced after Month 12 = 2027-10-14 based on progress)
  • Establish cell-level mass-and-volume model by Month 4 (2027-02-14); project Wh/kg and Wh/L for each chemistry starting Month 6 (2027-04-14); perform monthly updates and variance analysis by Month 20 (2028-06-14)
  • Commission pilot-line dry-room and pouch-cell fabrication line by Month 3 (2027-01-14); conduct trial builds and yield-optimization work Months 3-6 (2027-01-14 to 2027-04-14); reach target 50-100 cells/month by Month 24 (2028-10-14)
  • Establish forensics autopsy protocol and forensics atlas by Month 6 (2027-04-14); begin weekly failure analysis by Month 9 (2027-07-14)
  • Identify and contract with primary characterization partners (≥2) by Month 3 (2027-01-14); negotiate guaranteed turnaround (≤3 weeks) and schedule first external analysis by Month 9 (2027-07-14)
  • Define go/no-go criteria per chemistry by Month 18 (2028-04-14): specify cycle-life target (proposed ≥300 cycles), Wh/kg and Wh/L thresholds (≥500 Wh/kg, ≥950 Wh/L interim), safety onset threshold (≥120°C) and what counts as 'pass' at Month 30 (2029-04-14)

Membership:

  • Chemistry Lead 1 (lithium-sulfur pathway)
  • Chemistry Lead 2 (anode-free solid-state pathway)
  • Chemistry Lead 3 (conversion cathode or reserve pathway)
  • Synthesis Team Manager (precursor sourcing, material procurement, lab safety coordination)
  • Pilot-Line and Cell-Engineering Lead (pouch-cell design, fabrication, process control)
  • Characterization and Forensics Lead (operando and post-mortem analysis, failure-root-cause investigation)
  • Data and Modeling Engineer (cell-level mass-and-volume model maintenance, performance tracking, statistical analysis)

Decision Rights: Chemistry Leadership Team owns all decisions below USD 500K per chemistry per quarter and within approved tranches. Decides resource allocation among synthesis, characterization and pilot-line work; adjusts chemistry-team budgets by ≤15% per quarter without Steering Committee approval, provided total stay within approved tranches. Decides cell-build schedule, characterization priorities and failure-analysis focus. Escalates to Steering Committee: cost overruns (team spend >USD 500K/quarter), schedule slips >4 weeks, cycle-life data missing at gate thresholds, safety concerns (onset <120°C or non-reversible overcharge), and characterization queue delays >4 weeks.

Decision Mechanism: Chemistry Leadership Team (7 members) meets weekly; Leads and Manager form a core decision group. Decisions by consensus if possible; tie-breaker: Chemistry Lead 1 (lithium-sulfur, most mature path) casts deciding vote on inter-team resource allocation, Pilot-Line Lead decides on fabrication scheduling conflicts, Characterization Lead decides on characterization-access conflicts. Major within-team changes (>20% staffing shift, >USD 100K reallocation per month) require written justification to Steering Committee within 5 days. Monthly reports to Steering Committee include progress summary, risk flags and revised go/no-go trajectory.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly synthesis and characterization team meetings (within-team technical sync), monthly full Chemistry Leadership meetings with Steering Committee liaison, quarterly deep-dive reviews with Steering Committee (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 = 2027-01-14, 2027-04-14, 2027-07-14, 2027-10-14, 2028-04-14, 2028-10-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14, etc.). Emergency meetings if safety issue arises or characterization bottleneck threatens timeline.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Cell-build status: fabrication yield, cycle-test results, Wh/kg and Wh/L measurements against model, batch-to-batch variability (target 90% within ±10%)
  • Failure analysis: new failures diagnosed, root causes assigned, forensics atlas updated, design changes queued
  • Characterization queue and throughput: samples processed, turnaround time, any backlog or partner delays, escalation if needed
  • Chemistry-specific progress: synthesis scalability, electrolyte/interface stability, lithium-metal protection or other design focus per pathway
  • Go/no-go trajectory: quarterly assessment against Month 18, 30, 36 (2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14) criteria; updated projections if a chemistry is off-track
  • Safety and abuse testing: upcoming scheduled tests, results from thermal-ramp or contracted testing, onset temperatures, any threshold violations

Escalation Path: Chemistry Leadership escalates to Steering Committee: (i) any chemistry showing cycle-life <250 cycles at 80% by Month 24 (2028-10-14), (ii) thermal-runaway onset <100°C at any point, (iii) measured pouch-cell Wh/L projected to fall below 950 Wh/L by Month 30 (2029-04-14), (iv) characterization queue delays exceeding 4 weeks, (v) precursor supply delays >2 weeks, (vi) cost overruns >USD 500K/quarter per team. Escalates to red team directly if a measurement discrepancy arises that undermines gate credibility (e.g., Wh/kg claims not reproducible at ≥90% consistency). Escalates to Compliance Office any safety incident (burns, chemical spill, equipment failure in abuse chamber, EHS violation).

3. Independent Technical Verification and Assurance Group (Red Team)

Rationale for Inclusion: High-ambition R&D programmes with competition between teams and high stakes (gatekeeping a USD 90M tranche or chemistry selection) face pressure to overstate progress or hide negative data. An independent red team with explicit authority to replicate key results, challenge claims and delay gate decisions protects programme credibility, patent value and funder confidence. Red team operates outside core teams to avoid bias.

Responsibilities:

  • Replicate critical experimental results at each gate (Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14): build ≥1 independently chosen cell per chemistry team (or ≥3 for finalist), cycle per the original protocol and verify Wh/kg, Wh/L and cycle-life claims within ±10%
  • Challenge progress claims: review monthly Chemistry Leadership reports and flag any inconsistencies (e.g., Wh/kg reported in November contradicts October data, or claimed ≥950 Wh/L but actual measured value is 920 Wh/L) within 5 days
  • Verify gate-decision criteria are met before advancement: at Months 18, 30, 36 (2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14), independently confirm that go/no-go threshold (e.g., ≥500 Wh/kg measured on ≥3 replicates) is satisfied or not; report findings in writing ≥5 days before Steering Committee gate meeting
  • Audit cell-level mass-and-volume model methodology: review model assumptions (current-collector thickness, separator weight, inactive components), validate against actual pouch-cell teardowns (mass, volume, component count) quarterly, flag any deviations from physical reality
  • Manage forensics quality: review forensic root-cause assignments (e.g., is a claimed 'dendrite growth failure' supported by SEM evidence?); escalate unfounded or inconsistent root-cause narratives to Chemistry Lead for correction
  • Report directly to Steering Committee: monthly written summary of any discrepancies or concerns; gate-decision readiness memo ≥5 days before each gate

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Recruit red team members (2-3 external or internal non-core scientists with battery expertise) by Month 1 (2026-11-14); establish independence: no reporting to chemistry leads, separate budget, authority to request data and resources from core teams
  • Define replication protocol and acceptance criteria by Month 3 (2027-01-14): specify cell-build procedure (sourced materials, assembly by red-team personnel or independent third party), cycling protocol (discharge rate, temperature, cycle count) and measurement tolerance (±10% on Wh/kg, ±5% on Wh/L, ±5% on cycle-life retention)
  • Establish monthly data-review cadence: receive Chemistry Leadership monthly reports within 5 days of publication, issue flag memo within 10 days if discrepancies detected
  • Plan gate-verification timeline: identify ≥1 cell per team (or ≥3 for finalist) for replication ~4 weeks before gate meeting, issue replication results ≥5 days before Steering Committee meeting
  • Conduct initial audit of cell-level mass-and-volume model (Month 6 = 2027-04-14): review model code, assumptions and prior pouch-cell measurements; report comparison of modeled Wh/kg vs actual measured Wh/kg for prior benchmark cells
  • Set up forensics-quality review process (Month 9 = 2027-07-14): receive monthly forensics atlas updates from Chemistry Lead, spot-check ≥3 failure root-cause assignments per month against SEM/spectroscopy data

Membership:

  • Red Team Lead (external expert or senior scientist not embedded in core teams)
  • Electrochemistry Expert (post-doctoral or senior scientist: cell building, cycling, Wh/kg/L measurement)
  • Characterization Specialist (operando and post-mortem analysis, failure-root-cause validation)

Decision Rights: Red team has exclusive authority to delay a gate decision ≤3 weeks to complete verification if core-team data is incomplete or inconsistent. Red team can request access to any chemistry-team laboratory notebook, instrument calibration records, and characterization data to validate claims. Red team cannot override Steering Committee gate decisions but can flag unresolved discrepancies to Funder, forcing resolution before tranche release. Red team can recommend demotion of a chemistry if replication consistently fails (measured <90% of claimed Wh/kg or Wh/L) or cycle-life claim is not supported.

Decision Mechanism: Red team decisions by consensus among the 3 members. If disagreement arises (e.g., one member thinks replication passed, two think it failed), red-team lead casts deciding vote. Red team prepares written gate-readiness memo (pass/no-pass/conditional pass with required remediation) signed by all three members. Steering Committee may override red-team no-pass recommendation only with unanimous vote and written justification to Funder.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly internal red-team technical meetings (30 min sync on replication status, monthly data-review findings), monthly data-review prep meetings (1 hour to plan gate verifications), gate-verification sprints at Months 17, 29, 35 (2028-03-14, 2029-03-14, 2029-09-14) (2-3 weeks focused replication work leading into Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14 gates).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Monthly data-review findings: discrepancies flagged in Chemistry Leadership reports, follow-up required, clarification received from chemistry leads
  • Replication status: cells being built, cycling progress, preliminary Wh/kg/L and cycle-life results, on-track for gate-readiness memo delivery
  • Model audit results: comparison of cell-level mass-and-volume model projections vs actual measured pouch cells, model assumptions validated or requiring revision
  • Forensics quality spot-checks: failure root-cause assignments reviewed, SEM/spectroscopy evidence assessed, any unsupported claims flagged for correction
  • Gate-readiness decision: pass/no-pass/conditional recommendation, required remediation if conditional, planned communication to Steering Committee

Escalation Path: Red team escalates directly to Steering Committee (bypassing chemistry leads) any finding suggesting: (i) systematic overstatement of Wh/kg or Wh/L (measured <85% of claimed), (ii) cycle-life data not reproducible, (iii) safety concern (onset <100°C not disclosed), (iv) forensic root-cause narratives unsupported by data. Red team escalates to Funder within 48 hours any finding suggesting programme data integrity issue or deliberate misrepresentation. If red team replication consistently fails for a chemistry, red team recommends Steering Committee demote or eliminate that chemistry path independent of chemistry-team objections.

4. Compliance, EHS and Regulatory Affairs Office

Rationale for Inclusion: High-energy lithium-rich cells require synthesis of reactive metals, flammable electrolytes and toxic precursors, plus abuse testing (thermal runaway, nail penetration, overcharge) in specialized chambers. Overlapping EPA hazardous-waste, OSHA worker-safety, TCEQ environmental, and local (Austin Fire Authority) permitting rules create complex compliance risk. A serious incident (lithium-water fire, solvent spill, overcharge thermal runaway) could shut operations for months and jeopardize the USD 300M programme. Dedicated compliance governance ensures permitting, incident prevention, regulatory monitoring and rapid response.

Responsibilities:

  • Secure phased permits and licenses: Phase 1 dry-room and assembly (Month 3 = 2027-01-14), Phase 2 reactive-metal and solvent synthesis (Month 6 = 2027-04-14), Phase 3 abuse-test chambers (Month 9 = 2027-07-14); manage applications, regulator engagement and compliance conditions
  • Maintain hazardous-materials compliance: register as EPA hazardous-waste generator, contract licensed waste handler, maintain inventory of reactive metals (lithium, sodium), flammable solvents and toxic precursors, document quantities and disposal per EPA rules
  • Implement EHS operating model: document standard operating procedures for reactive-chemistry synthesis, dry-room operation, cell assembly, abuse testing and waste handling; train all staff quarterly; maintain incident log and corrective-action tracking
  • Conduct quarterly internal EHS audits: inspect lab facilities, verify compliance with permits, audit waste-handling practices, test emergency response (spill kits, fire suppression, evacuation), check equipment maintenance and calibration
  • Manage regulatory monitoring: retain external regulatory consultant to track federal (EPA, OSHA, DOT), state (TCEQ) and local (Austin Fire Authority) rule changes; assess impact on operations; propose adaptations or retrofits if needed
  • Coordinate third-party safety testing: schedule and oversee thermal-ramp screening (Months 3-6 = 2027-01-14 to 2027-04-14), contracted abuse tests (Months 6-12 = 2027-04-14 to 2027-10-14) and in-house abuse chambers (Month 18 = 2028-04-14 onwards); verify test protocols meet ASTM or equivalent standards

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Hire Chief EHS Officer (experienced battery-lab or chemical-manufacturing background) by Month 1 (2026-11-14); establish Compliance Office with initial 1-2 FTE
  • Conduct regulatory assessment by Month 2 (2026-12-14): map all applicable EPA, OSHA, TCEQ and local rules; document current gaps (if any) relative to planned chemistry and testing scope; identify permit categories and application timelines
  • Develop phased-permit strategy by Month 2 (2026-12-14): propose Phase 1 (dry-room, low-hazard assembly) by Month 3 (2027-01-14); Phase 2 (reactive synthesis) by Month 6 (2027-04-14); Phase 3 (abuse chambers) by Month 9 (2027-07-14); identify any showstoppers or long-lead items
  • Initiate regulator engagement (Austin Fire Authority, TCEQ) at Month 0 (2026-10-14), before formal applications, to build collaborative relationship and identify early concerns
  • Develop standard operating procedures (SOPs) for reactive chemistry, dry-room operation, waste handling and abuse testing by Month 6 (2027-04-14); review with regulatory consultant; distribute and train all staff
  • Establish incident-response protocol by Month 3 (2027-01-14): define roles (EHS lead, emergency coordinator, regulator notification), communication chain, remediation steps and incident-log documentation
  • Contract regulatory-monitoring consultant by Month 3 (2027-01-14); retain ongoing subscription to federal and state regulatory update services; establish quarterly regulatory-review meetings

Membership:

  • Chief EHS Officer (full-time)
  • Regulatory Affairs Manager (part-time or shared, ~0.5 FTE)
  • Laboratory Safety Coordinator (on-site, ~0.5 FTE, embedded in chemistry teams)
  • External EHS Advisory Committee (established by Month 6 = 2027-04-14): include representatives from Austin Fire Authority, TCEQ, a third-party safety consultant, and the programme's external technical advisor

Decision Rights: Chief EHS Officer has authority to halt any laboratory operation if safety or compliance concern arises (e.g., permit violation, improper chemical handling, equipment malfunction); halt remains in effect until remediated and approved by EHS Officer. Chief EHS Officer approves any synthesis of new chemical precursor or reactive material before first use on site, including review of hazard data sheets, storage requirements and waste-disposal plan. Chief EHS Officer approves in-house abuse-test protocols before chambers are commissioned. Regulatory Affairs Manager approves any external communications regarding environmental incidents or compliance status. Steering Committee must approve any decision to outsource on-site-prohibited chemistry synthesis (estimated cost USD 2-5M/yr if needed) or to defer permitting of planned facilities (e.g., delay abuse chambers from Month 9 = 2027-07-14 to Month 12 = 2027-10-14).

Decision Mechanism: Chief EHS Officer issues safety halt unilaterally if immediate danger is present; all other decisions by consensus with Regulatory Affairs Manager and Laboratory Safety Coordinator (3 required). If disagreement arises (e.g., EHS lead says chemistry must be outsourced, Chemistry Lead disagrees on hazard level), external EHS Advisory Committee member is consulted within 48 hours and their input informs final decision. Monthly EHS reports to Steering Committee document compliance status, any incidents (goal: zero), corrective actions and anticipated permitting milestones.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly EHS coordination meetings (30 min) with Chemistry Leadership Lab Safety Coordinator, monthly full Compliance Office meetings (1 hour), quarterly internal audits (2-3 days on site), annual external audit by third-party safety firm (2-3 days on site), quarterly regulator engagement meetings (with Austin Fire Authority, TCEQ representatives).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Permit status and timeline: Phase 1-3 application progress, regulator feedback, anticipated approval dates, any barriers or required adaptations
  • Compliance findings from quarterly internal audits: violations or near-misses, root causes, corrective actions and completion status
  • Incident log review: any chemical spills, equipment failures, near-misses, injuries; corrective actions taken and lessons learned
  • Regulatory-update monitoring: new EPA, OSHA, TCEQ or local rules affecting operations; impact assessment and required adaptations
  • Safety-testing status: scheduled thermal-ramp and abuse tests, protocol review, contractor qualifications, result review and any safety thresholds (proposed ≥120°C onset) met
  • Waste-handling and inventory: hazardous-waste streams, disposal routes, contractor compliance, chemical inventory accuracy checks against permits

Escalation Path: Chief EHS Officer escalates to Steering Committee (within 48 hours) any: (i) serious incident (fire, chemical release, equipment failure) causing injury or environmental exposure, (ii) regulatory notice of violation (NOV) or threatened permit revocation, (iii) discovery of non-compliance requiring costly retrofit or extended downtime, (iv) regulator demand for operational change (e.g., tighter dry-room control, equipment replacement). Chief EHS Officer escalates to external EHS Advisory Committee for input on complex hazard assessment (e.g., is a newly identified precursor allowable on site?) or permitting questions. Chief EHS Officer escalates to Funder within 72 hours any serious incident and remediation cost >USD 1M.

5. Finance and Funding Governance (Integrated within Steering Committee)

Rationale for Inclusion: The fixed USD 300M budget is divided into evidence-linked tranches (USD 60/80/70/90M) with USD 20M reserve and USD 15M pivot runway. Financial governance ensures tranche release is conditional on demonstrated milestones, spending stays within tranches and allocated reserves, and budget reallocation decisions are transparent and controlled. The opex-vs-tranche mismatch (average opex ~USD 33M/yr vs Months 36-84 = 2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14 tranche of ~USD 22.5M/yr) requires careful carry-forward management and partner co-funding coordination. Integrated within Steering Committee rather than standalone to ensure financial decisions align with technical gates.

Responsibilities:

  • Manage tranche release: T1 (USD 60M) released at project start Month 0 (2026-10-14); T2 (USD 80M) at Month 12 (2027-10-14) conditional on Phase 1 permit, operational pilot line and cell-level model live; T3 (USD 70M) at Month 24 (2028-10-14) conditional on Month 18 (2028-04-14) gate pass; T4 (USD 90M) at Month 36 (2029-10-14) conditional on chemistry selection gate and Month 30 (2029-04-14) pouch verification
  • Monitor spend against tranches: monthly dashboard of cumulative spend by budget category (payroll ~USD 70M, capital ~USD 50M, facility ~USD 25M, variable ~USD 135M), remaining tranche balance, variance from plan and pending reallocations; escalate any category >±15% of plan
  • Manage reserve (USD 20M unallocated) and pivot runway (USD 15M ring-fenced): hold unallocated and available for urgent redirects, pivots or cost overruns; release only with Steering Committee approval (>USD 1M requires unanimous vote); carry forward unused reserve through Month 30 (2029-04-14), available for later-stage contingencies
  • Coordinate partner co-funding (proposed ≥15% of shared costs): track partner financial and in-kind contributions (characterization access, graduate-student stipends, equipment loaning); verify deliverables are met; offset programme spend where applicable
  • Manage currency risk: identify major equipment and precursor purchases denominated in EUR or other foreign currency by Month 2 (2026-12-14); negotiate fixed-USD contracts or forward-exchange agreements for capital orders (Months 2-6 = 2026-12-14 to 2027-04-14); monitor EUR/USD rate; retain USD 2-3M currency contingency within the USD 5M general reserve

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish Finance Governance charter by Month 1 (2026-11-14): define tranche-release conditions, spend-approval authority (Director: <USD 500K/decision, Steering Committee: USD 500K-2M, Funder: >USD 2M or reserve activation), and variance thresholds (escalate if category >±15% of quarterly plan)
  • Develop detailed budget allocation model by Month 2 (2026-12-14): break down USD 300M by category and year (payroll, capital, facility lease, precursor and testing, EHS and computing, reserve); validate sum-to-total and identify any funding gaps
  • Set up monthly financial-tracking dashboard by Month 3 (2027-01-14): automated spend reporting by cost center (four chemistry teams, pilot line, characterization, EHS, computing, etc.), variance flagging (±15%) and tranche-balance tracking
  • Identify all major equipment and precursor purchases expected to be denominated in foreign currency (EUR, CNY, JPY) by Month 2 (2026-12-14); by Month 6 (2027-04-14), lock in fixed-USD pricing or forward-exchange contracts for capital equipment ordered in Months 2-6 (2026-12-14 to 2027-04-14)
  • Negotiate partner cost-sharing agreements by Month 3 (2027-01-14): formalize contributions (≥15% of shared characterization, materials and validation costs) in writing; establish invoicing and reconciliation process; integrate partner spend tracking into financial dashboard
  • Document spend-approval authority and escalation protocol by Month 1 (2026-11-14): establish approval matrices (Director approves <USD 500K, Steering Committee approves USD 500K-2M, Funder approves >USD 2M); require written justification for any variance >±15% or reallocation >USD 1M

Membership:

  • Chief Financial Officer or Finance Manager (part-time, ~0.5 FTE, reports to Steering Committee chair or Director)
  • Programme Controller (part-time or shared, ~0.3 FTE, manages monthly spend tracking and variance reporting)
  • Steering Committee members (Director, chemistry leads, external advisor, funder representative) hold joint responsibility for budget-allocation decisions

Decision Rights: Director (Steering Committee chair) approves individual spending decisions up to USD 500K without committee vote, provided cumulative monthly spend stays within approved chemistry-team or operational budgets. Steering Committee approves reallocation between budget categories (e.g., moving USD 1M from capital to payroll for higher hiring) if reallocation is <USD 2M and total spend stays within current tranche. Steering Committee approves tranche release contingent on documented milestone achievement (Phase 1 permit, cell-level model live, Month 18 = 2028-04-14 gate pass, etc.). Funder approves any decision to access reserve (>USD 1M) or to reallocate between tranches. Finance Manager flags any monthly spend variance >±15% within 5 days; if variance is projected to exceed ±20% by quarter-end, Finance Manager and Director jointly propose corrective action to Steering Committee.

Decision Mechanism: Monthly spend variance flagged by Finance Manager; if <±15%, no action required. If ±15% to ±20%, Director reviews and approves corrective action (e.g., spending freeze in a category, or approval to exceed category). If >±20%, escalated to Steering Committee for review and reallocation decision. Tranche release decisions require Steering Committee majority vote (4 of 7 members) plus Funder approval. Reserve activation (>USD 1M) requires Steering Committee unanimity.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly financial reviews (1 hour, first Thursday of each month) with Director and Finance Manager; quarterly full Steering Committee financial briefing included in regular Steering Committee agenda; ad-hoc escalations if variance >±20% or unplanned expense >USD 500K.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Monthly spend dashboard: cumulative spend by category, remaining balance in current tranche, variance from plan (<±15% normal, flag if ±15%-20%, escalate if >±20%)
  • Burn-rate trajectory: YTD spend, projected annualized burn, carry-forward to next tranche, any anticipated shortfalls
  • Variance explanations: if a category exceeds ±15%, Finance Manager explains reason (one-time purchase, hiring acceleration, cost inflation) and proposed mitigation
  • Tranche-release readiness: upcoming tranche (T2, T3, T4) milestone status (permit, gate pass, cell verification), evidence of readiness, planned release date and sign-off
  • Partner co-funding status: invoices received, in-kind contributions quantified, deliverables verified, balance of cost-sharing aligned with ≥15% target
  • Currency and procurement: status of major equipment orders and foreign-currency exposure, forward-contract status, any FX volatility requiring mitigation

Escalation Path: Finance Manager escalates to Director within 5 days if any monthly spend category exceeds ±15% of plan. Director escalates to Steering Committee within 1 week if variance >±20% or if corrective action requires reallocation >USD 1M. Steering Committee escalates to Funder within 3 days if variance suggests tranche depletion ahead of schedule or if programme is at risk of spending >USD 300M total. Finance Manager escalates to Steering Committee immediately if any evidence of financial irregularity (unsupported invoices, cost-shadowing, double-billing) is discovered.

Governance Implementation Plan

1. Project Sponsor confirms programme Director (chair of Scientific Steering Committee) and appoints four Chemistry Leads (one per active chemistry pathway, one for reserve chemistry management). Director and Leads are identified by name or role descriptor; appointment confirmation letter issued.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor (pre-existing funder authority; not yet a constituted committee)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0 (2026-10-14) (project week 1-2)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Appointment Confirmation Letter naming Director and four Chemistry Leads
  • Director acceptance memo
  • Chemistry Lead CVs and conflict-of-interest declarations

Dependencies:

  • Project Sponsor identified and authorized to commit funding
  • Recruitment of Director and Chemistry Leads completed or offers accepted

2. Project Sponsor formally appoints the independent red team members (2-3 external or internal non-core scientists) with explicit authority to replicate results, challenge claims and delay gate decisions. Red team members are selected for independence from core chemistry teams and report directly to the Scientific Steering Committee, not to chemistry leads.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor in consultation with appointed Director

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-14)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Red Team Member Appointment Letters (3 members)
  • Red Team Charter documenting independence, decision authority and escalation rights
  • Red Team member CVs and conflict-of-interest declarations

Dependencies:

  • Director appointed (Month 0 = 2026-10-14)
  • External expert advisors or senior scientists identified as candidates for red team

3. Project Sponsor appoints Chief EHS Officer and external regulatory/EHS consultant to lead hazardous-materials compliance, permitting and incident prevention. This role is filled before formal site selection to enable immediate regulator engagement.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor in consultation with appointed Director

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-14)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Chief EHS Officer Appointment Letter
  • EHS Consultant Engagement Letter (3-5 year contract with quarterly regulatory-update briefings)
  • Chief EHS Officer acceptance memo and initial 30-day plan

Dependencies:

  • Director appointed (Month 0 = 2026-10-14)
  • Budget USD 500K-1M/yr approved for EHS staff and consulting

4. Director drafts initial Terms of Reference (ToR) for the Scientific Steering Committee, including decision authority, meeting cadence (monthly Months 0-12 = 2026-10-14 to 2027-10-14, then quarterly), gate-review process (3-week cycles at Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14), escalation paths and conflict-resolution mechanisms. Draft incorporates lessons from the strategic-decisions document and risk-assessment framework.

Responsible Body/Role: Programme Director (appointed in Month 0 = 2026-10-14)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0 (2026-10-14), within 1 week of appointment

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Draft Scientific Steering Committee ToR v0.1
  • Proposed decision-authority matrix (Director: <USD 500K, Committee: USD 500K-2M, Funder: >USD 2M)
  • Proposed gate-review timeline and criteria checklist

Dependencies:

  • Director appointed (Month 0 = 2026-10-14)
  • Project Sponsor guidance on escalation paths and funder sign-off thresholds provided

5. Director circulates draft Scientific Steering Committee ToR for review and feedback from the nominated Chemistry Leads, external technical advisor and Funder representative. Review period is 1 week; feedback consolidated into a summary memo.

Responsible Body/Role: Programme Director

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0-1 (2026-10-14 to 2026-11-14), concurrent with ToR drafting

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • ToR Review Feedback Summary (consolidated from all reviewers)
  • Marked-up draft ToR v0.2 with Director responses to feedback

Dependencies:

  • Draft ToR v0.1 circulated (Month 0 = 2026-10-14)
  • Chemistry Leads, external advisor and Funder representative identified and available to review

6. Director finalizes Scientific Steering Committee ToR incorporating feedback and obtains sign-off from Funder representative. Final ToR is issued and shared with all Committee members.

Responsible Body/Role: Programme Director

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-14), by the end of the week

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Approved Scientific Steering Committee ToR v1.0
  • Funder sign-off email or memo
  • Distribution list and meeting-calendar invitations for first Committee meeting (Month 1 = 2026-11-14)

Dependencies:

  • ToR v0.2 and feedback summary completed (Month 0-1 = 2026-10-14 to 2026-11-14)
  • Funder representative acceptance of ToR authority levels

7. Chief EHS Officer and Director jointly engage Austin Fire Authority, Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) and EPA representatives in an initial collaborative meeting to outline the programme's chemistry scope, permitting needs (phased dry-room, synthesis, abuse-test chambers) and compliance strategy. Regulator feedback informs the phased-permit plan.

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Regulator Engagement Meeting Minutes (fire authority, TCEQ, EPA)
  • Regulator Feedback Summary (permit categories, application timelines, early concerns)
  • Preliminary Phased-Permit Plan (Phase 1-3 timeline and required applications)

  • Site location selected or under review (not yet required to be final)

Director and Finance Manager jointly develop a detailed budget-allocation model breaking down the USD 300M by category (payroll, capital, facility, precursor, testing, EHS, computing, reserve) and year. The model identifies any funding gaps, carry-forward requirements (Months 36-84 = 2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14 opex shortfall) and partner co-funding offset targets (proposed ≥15%).

Director and Chief EHS Officer jointly develop a comprehensive regulatory-compliance assessment covering EPA, OSHA, TCEQ, DOT and local Austin Fire Authority rules applicable to the programme's reactive-materials, synthesis and abuse-testing operations.   • External EHS consultant retained (Month 1 = 2026-11-14)

Criteria include quantified thresholds for cell-level energy density (≥500 Wh/kg, ≥950 Wh/L interim), cycle life (≥300 cycles at 80% retention, proposed threshold), safety (thermal-runaway onset ≥120°C, proposed), and cell-level mass-and-volume model reproducibility (90% of cells within ±10%, proposed). Criteria are documented in a Gate Criteria Specification document.
