Decision Escalation Matrix

Chemistry Tournament Failure or No Viable Path to 500 Wh/kg at Cell Level Escalation Level: Scientific Steering Committee with Funder Review Approval Process: Steering Committee majority vote (4 of 7 members) to recommend chemistry deprioritization, pivot to reserve, or programme descope. Funder approval required if descope involves release of T4 (USD 90M) or if proceeding with only one candidate instead of two finalists at Month 36 (2029-10-14). Rationale: A staged chemistry tournament is the core hedging strategy against dead-end chemistry risk. If two of three active chemistries fail fundamental feasibility (cycle-life collapse, dendrite growth, volume expansion) by Month 30 (2029-04-14), escalation is mandatory to activate reserve chemistry or decide whether to stop. Without escalation, wasted investment on non-viable paths consumes USD 5–10 M and compresses final-stage work from 48 to 38–42 months. Negative Consequences: Unmanaged chemistry failure at Month 36 (2029-10-14) leaves only one or no viable finalist, forcing either a desperate pivot with 38–42 months remaining (insufficient for proof-of-concept and licensing readiness) or programme stop without a deliverable. Failure to escalate early (before Month 30 = 2029-04-14) costs USD 10–20 M in sunk effort and delays final proof 6–12 months, jeopardizing the Month 84 (2033-10-14) delivery date.

Volumetric Energy Density Falls Below 950 Wh/L Interim Threshold or Projected Below 1000 Wh/L at Month 30 (2029-04-14) Escalation Level: Scientific Steering Committee with Chemistry Leadership and Red Team Input Approval Process: Steering Committee majority vote to authorize a 6-month focused architecture sprint (Months 30–36 = 2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14) to address volumetric penalties via thinner separators, higher-density cathode, or bipolar/anode-free format; reallocation of USD 8–15 M (estimate) from other budget categories; or deprioritization of the affected chemistry. Funder sign-off if reallocation exceeds USD 5 M. Rationale: The 1000 Wh/L target is as challenging as 500 Wh/kg but receives secondary priority in early discovery work. Material-level energy density often collapses at cell level once separator thickness, electrolyte volume and packaging overhead are included. Discovering volumetric penalties late (after Month 36 = 2029-10-14 selection gate) leaves insufficient time for redesign; escalation at Month 30 (2029-04-14) allows 6-month corrective sprint before final selection. Negative Consequences: If volumetric shortfall is not escalated and addressed by Month 36 (2029-10-14), final delivery at Month 72 (2032-10-14) may achieve 500 Wh/kg but only 800–900 Wh/L, reducing invention value and licensing appeal by 30–40%. Programme credibility is damaged if a headline 1000 Wh/L goal is missed due to late recognition of packaging penalties. Redesign cost and timeline slip compress the Months 36–84 (2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14) optimization window from 48 to 36–42 months.

Site Permitting Delayed More Than 6 Months or Phase 1 Permit Denied Escalation Level: Chief EHS Officer to Steering Committee to Funder (Critical Path Risk) Approval Process: Chief EHS Officer escalates permit status to Steering Committee within 48 hours of learning of any delay >4 weeks or regulator notice of denial. Steering Committee authorizes contingency measures within 1 week: (i) pre-negotiated external synthesis partnerships (cost USD 2–5 M/yr, 4–6 week turnarounds) to continue chemistry work; (ii) deferral of Phase 2 synthesis to external vendors; (iii) revision of operational timeline and T2 release milestone tied to actual permit approval rather than Month 12 (2027-10-14) target. Funder approval required if delay compresses effective programme duration below 75 months or if external-synthesis costs exceed USD 10 M total. Rationale: Permitting is on the critical path: a 6–8 month slip (plausible given overlapping EPA, TCEQ and local fire-authority processes) reduces effective work time from 84 to 76–78 months, compressing chemistry selection and final proof timelines. Phase 1 denial (dry-room/assembly operations) blocks operational start entirely. Escalation enables rapid contingency activation: pre-negotiated external synthesis partnerships allow chemistry work to continue even if on-site synthesis is prohibited. Negative Consequences: Unmanaged permitting delay of 6–8 months pushes operational start from Month 3 (2027-01-14) to Month 9 (2027-07-14), leaving only 75 effective work months. Month 36 (2029-10-14) chemistry-selection gate compresses from 48 remaining months to 39–42 months for final proof-of-concept, risking incomplete validation or forced descope to 480 Wh/kg instead of 500. Phase 1 denial without contingency halts all operations, consuming USD 30–50 M in sunk facility and equipment capital with no recovery. External synthesis at USD 2–5 M/yr consumes USD 10–25 M over 5–7 years (5–8% of budget).

Pilot-Line Capital Commitment Decision Unresolved or Build Overruns Beyond USD 15 M Budget Escalation Level: Finance Manager and Programme Director to Scientific Steering Committee Approval Process: Finance Manager flags by Month 1 (2026-11-14) that pilot-line decision (build vs. lease vs. modular) is the single largest capital commitment before chemistry is proven. Steering Committee majority vote is required to approve any option exceeding USD 15 M or with <3-year lead time. If procurement quotes exceed USD 15 M, Director requests recompetition or reduced scope; if overrun is unavoidable, Steering Committee must approve reallocation from other capital categories (e.g., reducing characterization instrument spending) or requesting additional budget (triggering Funder escalation). Rationale: A new-build owned pilot line costs USD 30–50 M and requires 6–12 month lead time, consuming 10–17% of total budget and 12 months of programme time before chemistry is even selected. Building now locks capital before chemistry risk is resolved and creates stranded-asset risk if winning chemistry has incompatible drying or pressure requirements. Leasing (USD 0.6–1.2 M/yr operating cost, ~USD 4–8 M over 7 years) preserves flexibility and capital for pivots. Unresolved decision delays first pouch-cell builds by 6–12 months, compressing discovery loop. Negative Consequences: If build option is selected without escalation and later the winning chemistry requires different conditions, USD 30–50 M of equipment is partially stranded, reducing effective budget to USD 250–270 M (13–17% loss). Build timeline slippage of 6–12 months defers first pouch cells to Month 9–12 (2027-07-14 to 2027-10-14), losing discovery iterations in Months 3–9 (2027-01-14 to 2027-07-14). Leasing with queue delays of 4–8 weeks slows hypothesis testing by 50%, reducing annual candidate throughput by ~50%.

Cycle-Life or Safety Threshold Violated: Measured <250 Cycles or Thermal Runaway Onset <100°C Escalation Level: Red Team to Chemistry Leadership to Scientific Steering Committee (Technical Gate Risk) Approval Process: Red Team flags any chemistry candidate with measured cycle-life <250 cycles at 80% retention or thermal-runaway onset <100°C within 5 days of data receipt. Chemistry Lead responds within 3 days with either: (i) a documented redesign plan (interface engineering, cathode doping, electrolyte additives) with timeline and success criteria; or (ii) recommendation to deprioritize or stop. If redesign plan is credible and within 2–4 months, Steering Committee approves continued investment. If plan is not credible or redesign would consume >USD 2 M additional, Steering Committee authorizes deprioritization and budget reallocation to remaining active chemistries. Rationale: Cycle-life <300 cycles (proposed threshold) and thermal-runaway onset <120°C are hard failure modes that make a cell non-commercial regardless of energy density. A cell meeting 500 Wh/kg but degrading below 80% capacity in 150 cycles or experiencing thermal runaway at 90°C is worse than useless—it is dangerous. Escalation enforces discipline: unmet cycle-life data by Month 24 (2028-10-14) or safety violations at any point trigger mandatory redesign or deprioritization before capital is wasted on optimization. Negative Consequences: If cycle-life or safety violations are not escalated and addressed early, a failing chemistry can consume 6–12 months of effort and USD 5–10 M in pilot-line, characterization and optimization costs before being abandoned at Month 30 (2029-04-14) or later. A chemistry that passes energy-density targets but fails safety certification late forces either immediate deprioritization or a risky decision to accept marginal safety. Unmanaged safety discovery late in the programme (Month 48+) could trigger facility permitting revision (costs USD 2–5 M, 3–4 month downtime).

Budget Overrun or Spend Variance >20% in Any Category or Tranche Depletion Forecast Escalation Level: Finance Manager to Steering Committee to Funder (Financial Gate) Approval Process: Finance Manager flags monthly spend variance >15% within 5 days; if variance reaches 15–20%, Director proposes corrective action (spending freeze in a category, or one-time reallocation <USD 1 M). If variance exceeds 20% or is projected to persist, escalated to Steering Committee majority vote for reallocation decision (internal to current tranche, up to USD 2 M). If reallocation >USD 2 M or involves inter-tranche carry-forward shortfall, Funder approval required. Tranche depletion forecast (spending projected to exceed tranche balance >4 months before next tranche release) triggers Steering Committee review and Funder notification within 2 weeks. Rationale: The fixed USD 300 M budget is divided into tranches (USD 60/80/70/90 M) with USD 20 M unallocated reserve. A 20% overrun in any major category (payroll USD 10 M/yr, capital USD 50 M, facility USD 25 M) compresses working capital by USD 2–10 M, threatening mid-stage pivots or final-stage optimization. Permitting delays, staff attrition, equipment cost inflation or partner loss can each add USD 2–5 M unbudgeted cost. Escalation enables rapid reallocation or Funder negotiation before spend gaps compromise programme viability. Negative Consequences: Unmanaged budget overruns of 15–20% across Months 0–36 (2026-10-14 to 2029-10-14) leave only USD 240–255 M for critical Months 36–84 (2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14) work, reducing annual burn capacity from ~USD 33 M to ~USD 26–28 M (20–25% reduction). Front-loaded capital overruns (facility USD 30–50 M build instead of USD 15 M lease, USD 10 M characterization instruments vs. USD 2–3 M, USD 5–10 M hiring overages) compress chemistry work and optimization budgets in later years. A 10–15% cumulative overrun forces either scaling back of Months 36–84 (early stop before full proof-of-concept) or Funder request for additional funds (ruptures fixed-budget constraint).

Monitoring Progress

1. Tracking Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) against Project Plan and Chemistry-Tournament Milestones

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Project Governance Dashboard (technical, financial, schedule and risk metrics updated monthly)
  • Chemistry-Tournament Progress Tracking Spreadsheet (cell builds, Wh/kg, Wh/L, cycle-life data per pathway)
  • Cell-Level Mass-and-Volume Model with Monthly Updates (projected vs. measured energy density, variance analysis)
  • Monthly Chemistry Leadership Progress Report Template (cell-build count, measurements, forensics findings, gate-criteria tracking)

Frequency: Weekly synthesis/characterization team sync meetings; monthly Chemistry Leadership progress reports; quarterly full Scientific Steering Committee reviews (monthly in Months 0-12 = 2026-10-14 to 2027-10-14); gate-review cycles at Months 18, 30, 36 (2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14)

Responsible Role: Chemistry and Discovery Leadership Team (Chemistry Leads, Data Engineer, Pilot-Line Manager) with oversight by Programme Director and Scientific Steering Committee

Adaptation Process: Monthly progress data is reviewed by Chemistry Leadership and Steering Committee liaison. If a chemistry pathway is off-track against interim targets (projected Wh/kg, Wh/L, cycle-life or safety thresholds), Chemistry Leads propose corrective actions (materials redesign, electrolyte optimization, pilot-line process adjustment, characterization focus shift). Corrective actions up to USD 500K/quarter are approved by Chemistry Leads within their authority; larger redirects are escalated to Steering Committee for authorization. Quarterly Steering Committee reviews assess all three pathways against gate criteria and recommend budget rebalancing or deprioritization if progress diverges significantly. At formal gates (Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14), Steering Committee renders go/no-go decisions per chemistry based on documented evidence.

Adaptation Trigger: Monthly data variance >15% from quarterly projection triggers Chemistry Lead review and proposed corrective action within 5 days. Cumulative Wh/kg or Wh/L variance >10% by Month 20 (2028-06-14) initiates model recalibration. Any chemistry failing to meet Month 18 (2028-04-14) interim targets (cycle-life <250 cycles measured, thermal-runaway onset <100°C, Wh/L <900 projected at cell level) is flagged for deprioritization. Any chemistry with measured cycle-life <250 cycles at 80% retention by Month 24 (2028-10-14) is recommended for deprioritization at Month 30 (2029-04-14) gate unless redesign is within 2-4 months. Gate criteria not met by Month 30 (2029-04-14) (≥500 Wh/kg AND ≥950 Wh/L third-party verified, ≥300 cycles at 80%, thermal-runaway onset ≥120°C) trigger contingency evaluation: pivot to reserve chemistry or extended redesign sprint (Months 30-36 = 2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14) before final selection gate.

2. Independent Technical Verification and Red-Team Challenge of Progress Claims

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Red Team Replication Protocol and Cell-Build Documentation (independent replication of 1+ cell per chemistry per gate)
  • Monthly Data-Review Flag Memo (discrepancies flagged by red team within 10 days of Chemistry Leadership monthly reports)
  • Red-Team Verification Results Memo (gate readiness assessment, pass/no-pass on replication tolerance ±10% Wh/kg, ±5% Wh/L)
  • Red-Team Gate-Readiness Certification Memo (final recommendation on chemistry finalist selection at each gate: Month 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14)

Frequency: Monthly data-review cycles (red team review of Chemistry Leadership monthly reports within 10 days, flag memo issued within 5 days if discrepancies detected); gate-verification sprints at Months 17, 29, 35 (2028-03-14, 2029-03-14, 2029-09-14) leading into Months 18, 30, 36 (2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14) gates (2-3 week replication period per gate); cell-level mass-and-volume model audit monthly with formal comparison to measured pouch-cell teardowns quarterly

Responsible Role: Independent Red Team (2-3 external or internal non-core scientists, reporting directly to Scientific Steering Committee, not to Chemistry Leads); Red-Team Lead coordinates replication protocol and monthly data review

Adaptation Process: Monthly data-review flag memos are circulated to Chemistry Leads, who respond within 3 days with clarification or correction of any claimed inconsistencies (e.g., Wh/kg measured in November contradicts October data, or claimed Wh/L falls below projected threshold). Unresolved discrepancies are escalated to Steering Committee within 1 week for adjudication. At gate reviews (Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14), red-team replication results (pass/no-pass on acceptance criteria: ±10% Wh/kg, ±5% Wh/L, ±5% cycle-life retention, proposed) determine gate-readiness status. If red-team replication consistently fails (measured <90% of claimed Wh/kg or Wh/L), the affected chemistry is flagged for Steering Committee review; Steering Committee may recommend deprioritization independent of Chemistry Leads' objections. If red-team identifies systematic data-quality issues or measurement methodology problems, gate decision is delayed up to 3 weeks to allow remedial verification before Steering Committee renders final go/no-go.

Adaptation Trigger: Monthly data discrepancies flagged by red team within 10 days of Chemistry Leadership report; Chemistry Lead response required within 3 days. Unresolved inconsistencies (Chemistry Lead cannot explain variance, or flag is not addressed) escalate to Steering Committee within 1 week. Red-team replication results differing by >10% Wh/kg or >5% Wh/L from claimed values delay gate decision up to 3 weeks for root-cause investigation. Red-team finding of <80% reproducibility (fewer than ~7 of 10 replicates meeting claimed Wh/kg and Wh/L within tolerance) triggers recommendation to deprioritize that chemistry at the next gate (Month 18, 30 or 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14).

3. Cycle-Life and Safety-Threshold Monitoring Against Hard Gate Criteria

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Monthly Cycle-Life Performance Report (measured cycles at 80% retention per chemistry, trend tracking, redesign actions flagged)
  • Safety-Test Results Database (thermal-ramp screening results, contracted abuse-test reports, in-house chamber data)
  • Cycle-Life Deprioritization Decision Log (any chemistry <250 cycles at 80%, documented, flagged for gate review)
  • Safety Threshold Compliance Tracker (thermal-runaway onset temperature, overcharge reversibility, cells failing thresholds)

Frequency: Monthly cycle-life data collection and trending (as cells complete cycling tests, typically 1-6 months per cell depending on test protocol); thermal-ramp screening monthly Months 3-6 (2027-01-14 to 2027-04-14); contracted abuse testing at designated milestones (Months 6, 9, 12 = 2027-04-14, 2027-07-14, 2027-10-14 estimated); in-house abuse chamber testing quarterly once commissioned (Months 18+ = 2028-04-14 onward)

Responsible Role: Chemistry Leads and Characterization Manager (cycle-life data tracking); Chief EHS Officer and external safety consultant (abuse-test scheduling and results review); Safety data flagged to Steering Committee monthly via Chemistry Progress Report

Adaptation Process: Monthly cycle-life report trends are reviewed by Chemistry Leadership and flagged to Steering Committee if any candidate shows measured retention falling toward <250 cycles at 80%. Chemistry Lead responds with redesign action plan (interface engineering, cathode doping, electrolyte additive, cell format adjustment) and estimated timeline to recovery (typically 2-4 months for one iteration). If redesign is credible and within 2-4 months, continued investment is approved. If redesign is not credible or would require >6 months, Steering Committee authorizes deprioritization and budget reallocation to remaining active chemistries. Safety-test results (thermal-ramp onset, abuse-test performance) are reviewed by Chemistry Leadership and EHS Officer; any cell with onset <100°C or non-reversible overcharge failure is flagged immediately for Chemistry Lead investigation. If a leading chemistry fails safety threshold and cannot be corrected within 2-4 months, deprioritization is recommended at the next gate (Month 18, 30 or 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14).

Adaptation Trigger: Measured cycle-life <250 cycles at 80% retention detected at any point; Chemistry Lead must provide redesign plan within 3 days. Lack of credible redesign plan or failure to achieve ≥300 cycles by Month 24 (2028-10-14) triggers deprioritization recommendation at Month 30 (2029-04-14) gate. Thermal-runaway onset <100°C or failure to reverse after overcharge triggers immediate escalation to Chief EHS Officer and Steering Committee; decision on deprioritization or emergency redesign within 1 week. Any safety threshold violation at Month 30 (2029-04-14) gate or later disqualifies chemistry from finalist selection unless onset can be raised to ≥120°C (proposed threshold) within the gate-to-selection window (Months 30-36 = 2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14).

4. Volumetric Energy Density (1000 Wh/L) Parity Monitoring and Cell-Architecture Optimization Triggers

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Volumetric Density Focus List (monthly update of candidates projected <950 Wh/L interim threshold, flagged for redesign)
  • Cell-Level Mass-and-Volume Model (separator thickness, electrolyte volume, current-collector mass, inactive-mass breakdown tracked per candidate)
  • Wh/L Mismatch Root-Cause Analysis (model assumptions vs. measured pouch-cell teardowns, separator thickness bias, electrolyte volume overestimate)
  • Volumetric-Density Optimization Sprint Plan (if Month 30 = 2029-04-14 data shows chemistry meeting ≥500 Wh/kg but <950 Wh/L, dedicated 6-month architecture sprint authorized Months 30-36 = 2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14)

Frequency: Quarterly volumetric-density review (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 = 2027-01-14, 2027-04-14, 2027-07-14, 2027-10-14, 2028-04-14, 2028-10-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14); monthly model updates incorporating actual measured cell-level Wh/kg and Wh/L; pouch-cell teardown mass-and-volume audits conducted on 2-3 representative cells quarterly (Months 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30 = 2027-04-14, 2027-07-14, 2027-10-14, 2028-04-14, 2028-10-14, 2029-04-14) to validate model assumptions

Responsible Role: Chemistry Leads and Data Engineer; red team audits model assumptions and validates model-to-reality accuracy quarterly

Adaptation Process: If any chemistry is projected to fall below 950 Wh/L interim threshold by Month 18 (2028-04-14), Chemistry Lead initiates focused volumetric-density redesign: thinner separators, reduced electrolyte volume, higher-density cathode materials, or bipolar/anode-free cell-architecture evaluation. Progress on volumetric redesign is tracked monthly. By Month 24 (2028-10-14), all leading candidates must project ≥950 Wh/L or deprioritization is recommended. If Month 30 (2029-04-14) third-party verification shows a leading chemistry meeting ≥500 Wh/kg but measured Wh/L is <950 Wh/L (e.g., 920 Wh/L), Steering Committee authorizes a focused 6-month architecture sprint (Months 30-36 = 2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14) to close the gap through cell-format optimization (bipolar stacking, pressure management, anode-free architecture). Sprint goal is to recover Wh/L to ≥950 Wh/L by Month 36 (2029-10-14). If volumetric gap cannot be closed, the chemistry may still advance if Wh/kg target (≥500) is met, but with a conditional notation that the 1000 Wh/L target (final, not interim) is at risk.

Adaptation Trigger: Any chemistry projected <950 Wh/L interim at Month 18 (2028-04-14) gate triggers focused redesign work through Month 24 (2028-10-14). If chemistry is still projected <950 Wh/L at Month 24 (2028-10-14), deprioritization is recommended. If Month 30 (2029-04-14) measured Wh/L is <950 Wh/L for a leading chemistry (even if ≥500 Wh/kg), Steering Committee decision is required: either authorize a 6-month volumetric sprint (Months 30-36 = 2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14) with reallocation of USD 8-15 M (estimate) and adjusted timeline to final proof, or deprioritize the chemistry if arc-focused redesign is deemed infeasible. If final measured Wh/L at Month 72 (2032-10-14) is <950 Wh/L (falling short of 1000 Wh/L target), the invention is delivered as a partial success (500+ Wh/kg achieved, 1000 Wh/L missed), with documented root causes and design constraints.

5. Third-Party Verification and Cell-Level Proof-of-Concept Milestones

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Third-Party Pouch-Cell Testing Protocol and Laboratory Contract (independent laboratory or university partner, measurement certification)
  • Third-Party Verification Report (Month 30 = 2029-04-14: measured ≥500 Wh/kg, ≥950 Wh/L, ≥300 cycles at 80%, reproducibility ≥90% within ±10% Wh/kg, ±5% Wh/L)
  • Phase 1 Independent Verification Report (Month 12 = 2027-10-14: early-stage candidate cells tested to confirm in-house measurement methodology)
  • Final Programme Goal Certification Report (Month 72 = 2032-10-14: third-party verification of final cells meeting ≥500 Wh/kg, ≥1000 Wh/L, ≥300 cycles, ≥120°C thermal onset)

Frequency: Phase 1 independent verification of early-stage candidate cells: Months 9-12 (2027-07-14 to 2027-10-14); Month 30 (2029-04-14) third-party pouch-cell verification of finalist(s): testing conducted Months 26-30 (2028-12-14 to 2029-04-14) with results delivered by Month 30 (2029-04-14); final third-party certification at Months 60-72 (2031-10-14 to 2032-10-14) for delivery-ready cells

Responsible Role: Chemistry Leads coordinate cell selection and documentation for third-party testing; independent third-party laboratory (accredited testing organization or university partner) performs measurements and provides certified results; red team may independently verify third-party methodology or re-test if questions arise

Adaptation Process: Phase 1 independent verification (Month 12 = 2027-10-14) results are compared to in-house measurements. If systematic discrepancies emerge (e.g., in-house measurements consistently report Wh/kg 5-10% higher than third-party), in-house calibration procedures are reviewed and corrected by Month 15 (2028-01-14) so future measurements align with third-party standard. Month 30 (2029-04-14) third-party pouch-cell verification gates the chemistry-selection decision: Steering Committee go/no-go determination is conditional on third-party data confirming ≥500 Wh/kg AND ≥950 Wh/L in the same ≥3 replicates, ≥300 cycles at 80%, and 90% of cells within ±10% Wh/kg tolerance (proposed). If third-party verification shows measured values falling short of these thresholds (e.g., ≥480 Wh/kg but only ≥920 Wh/L, or <270 cycles), Steering Committee triggers either a 6-month redesign sprint (Months 30-36 = 2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14) or deprioritization of that chemistry. Final third-party certification (Months 60-72 = 2031-10-14 to 2032-10-14) confirms delivery-readiness; if final cells do not meet stated goals (≥500 Wh/kg, ≥1000 Wh/L final target, ≥300 cycles, ≥120°C thermal onset), Steering Committee documents partial success or descope decision.

Adaptation Trigger: Phase 1 independent verification results (Month 12 = 2027-10-14) differ by >5% Wh/kg or >3% Wh/L from in-house measurements trigger in-house methodology review and calibration by Month 15 (2028-01-14). Month 30 (2029-04-14) third-party data showing measured <500 Wh/kg or <950 Wh/L in the finalist chemistry triggers Steering Committee decision on 6-month sprint (reallocation of USD 8-15 M) or deprioritization. Third-party verification of <90% reproducibility (fewer than ~7 of 10 replicates meeting ±10% tolerance) flags cell-build quality issues; Chemistry Lead provides corrective action plan for pilot-line process improvement by Month 32 (2029-06-14). Final certification (Month 72 = 2032-10-14) showing Wh/L <950 Wh/L (falling short of 1000 Wh/L) is documented; if Wh/kg meets ≥500 and cycle-life meets ≥300 cycles, delivery may proceed as partial success with noted constraint; if either Wh/kg or cycle-life falls short, programme escalates to Funder for final delivery decision.

6. Risk Register and Contingency Management Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Project Risk Register (20+ identified risks covering chemistry pathway, volumetric density, permitting, budget/burn, talent, partnerships, supply chain, regulatory, IP, manufacturing, cycle-life degradation)
  • Monthly Risk Dashboard (risk status: green/yellow/red, escalations in month, mitigation actions tracked by owner and due date)
  • Contingency Pivot Plan per Chemistry Pathway (precursor sourcing, pilot-line equipment reconfiguration, staff cross-training status)
  • Pivot-Runway Reserve Allocation Tracking (USD 15 M ring-fenced until Month 36 = 2029-10-14 gate, available for emergency redirects if two of three active chemistries fail)

Frequency: Risk register initialized at Month 1 (2026-11-14); monthly risk review with Chemistry Leadership (risk status update, mitigation progress tracking); quarterly full Steering Committee risk briefing (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 = 2027-01-14, 2027-04-14, 2027-07-14, 2027-10-14, 2028-04-14, 2028-10-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14); escalation within 48 hours if a risk approaches trigger threshold (e.g., permitting delay exceeds 4 weeks, budget variance >15%, partner access delayed >3 weeks, chemistry fails cycle-life test)

Responsible Role: Programme Director maintains master risk register; Chemistry Leads own technical risks and mitigation actions; Chief EHS Officer owns permitting and regulatory risks; Finance Manager owns budget and cost-overrun risks; Programme Director escalates risks to Scientific Steering Committee when trigger threshold is approached

Adaptation Process: Monthly risk reviews identify which risks are trending toward trigger thresholds. Chemistry Leads propose mitigation actions (e.g., increased synthesis effort if a chemistry's cycle-life is approaching <250 cycles threshold, or pre-staging reserve chemistry if two active chemistries show fundamental limitations). Mitigation actions up to USD 500K are approved by Chemistry Leads; larger actions (contingency activation, major budget reallocation) require Steering Committee approval. At gate reviews (Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14), Steering Committee assesses whether any open risks have crystallized into hard failures (chemistry no longer viable, permitting denied, partner lost) and triggers contingency plans (pivot to reserve chemistry, activate outsourced synthesis, draw on pivot-runway reserve, extend timeline). Pivot-runway reserve (USD 15 M) is held unallocated until Month 30 (2029-04-14); if a chemistry fails between Months 18-30 (2028-04-14 to 2029-04-14), Steering Committee may authorize release of USD 5-10 M to support rapid pivot activation (precursor procurement, equipment reconfiguration, staff retraining for reserve chemistry) to minimize schedule slip.

Adaptation Trigger: Any risk trending toward or exceeding trigger threshold (e.g., permitting delay >4 weeks, monthly spend variance >15%, chemistry cycle-life <250 cycles, thermal-runaway onset falling below 100°C, partner access queue delay >3 weeks, attrition exceeding 15%/yr) is escalated by the owning team (Chemistry Lead, EHS Officer, Finance Manager, Talent Lead) to Steering Committee within 5 days of threshold breach. Steering Committee convenes within 1 week to review trigger status and authorize mitigation or contingency activation. For chemistry-related risks (pathway failure, cycle-life collapse, safety threshold breach, volumetric-density shortfall), deprioritization of the affected chemistry or reserve-chemistry activation is decided at the next formal gate (Month 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14) or earlier if the risk crystallizes into confirmed failure. For operational risks (permitting denial, partner loss, supply-chain disruption), contingency measures (external synthesis activation, backup partner engagement, material re-sourcing) are implemented immediately upon Steering Committee authorization.

7. Financial Tracking and Budget-Reallocation Governance

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Monthly Financial-Tracking Dashboard (cumulative spend by cost center: payroll, capital, facility, precursor, testing, EHS, computing, reserve; remaining tranche balance; variance flagging if category >±15% of plan)
  • Tranche Release Decision Package and Evidence Checklist (T2 at Month 12 = 2027-10-14 conditional on Phase 1 permit, operational pilot line, live cell-level model; T3 at Month 24 = 2028-10-14 conditional on Month 18 = 2028-04-14 gate pass; T4 at Month 36 = 2029-10-14 conditional on chemistry-selection gate)
  • Quarterly Financial Review Report (cumulative spend, burn-rate profile, carry-forward forecast, partner cost-sharing reconciliation)
  • Currency Risk and Procurement Tracking (FX exposure on equipment orders, forward-exchange contract status, budget impact forecast)

Frequency: Monthly spend tracking and variance flagging (first Thursday of each month, within 5 days of month-end close); Director-Finance Manager monthly financial review (1 hour, variance discussion and corrective-action proposals if >15%); quarterly full Steering Committee financial briefing included in regular Steering Committee meeting agenda (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 = 2027-01-14, 2027-04-14, 2027-07-14, 2027-10-14, 2028-04-14, 2028-10-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14); ad-hoc escalation if spend variance exceeds 20% in any month or if tranche depletion is forecast >4 months early

Responsible Role: Finance Manager tracks monthly spend and updates dashboard; Director reviews variance and proposes corrective action; Steering Committee approves budget reallocations >USD 1 M or affecting inter-tranche timing; Funder approves release of each tranche (T2, T3, T4) and any reallocation >USD 2 M or reserve activation >USD 1 M

Adaptation Process: Monthly spend variance <±15% is flagged but requires no immediate action. Variance ±15% to ±20% is reviewed by Director and Finance Manager within 5 days; if variance is projected to persist (trend analysis), Director proposes corrective action: spending freeze in an overrunning category, one-time reallocation of unspent balance from another category, or revised spend forecast. Variance >20% or projected tranche depletion >4 months early is escalated to Steering Committee within 1 week for reallocation decision. Reallocation within current tranche and <USD 1 M is approved by Director; reallocation >USD 1 M or affecting inter-tranche timing (e.g., carrying forward underspend from T1 to cover T2 shortfall) requires Steering Committee majority vote. Tranche release conditions are verified by Finance Manager and Director before authorization memo is sent to Funder (typically 2-3 weeks before month of intended release). If release conditions are not met (e.g., Phase 1 permit not approved, cell-level model not live), tranche release is deferred and revised schedule is communicated to Funder. Partner cost-sharing reconciliation is conducted quarterly (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 = 2027-01-14 onwards): partner invoices are verified against contribution commitments; any under-contribution by partners (falling below ≥15% proposed target) triggers partner discussion and revised commitment or Steering Committee decision to absorb shortfall from programme budget.

Adaptation Trigger: Monthly spend category variance ±15-20% flagged by Finance Manager within 5 days; Director proposes corrective action within 10 days (spending freeze, one-time reallocation <USD 1 M, or revised forecast). Variance >20% or trend toward tranche depletion >4 months early escalates to Steering Committee within 1 week; Steering Committee votes within 3 days on reallocation decision (reallocate from another category, extend tranche timeline, or request Funder top-up if cap overrun is unavoidable). Tranche release condition not met (Phase 1 permit pending, cell-level model delay, Month 18 = 2028-04-14 gate inconclusive) triggers Steering Committee decision on defer release or proceed conditionally; Funder must approve any conditional release. FX exposure on equipment orders exceeding USD 10 M triggers forward-exchange contract negotiation; if contract cost exceeds USD 500K, Steering Committee approval is required.

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. Completeness Confirmation: All five core governance components (Stage 2 internal bodies, Stage 3 implementation plan, Stage 4 escalation matrix, Stage 5 monitoring, Stage 1 audit details) are present and documented. The framework includes Scientific Steering Committee, Chemistry Leadership Team, Independent Red Team, EHS/Compliance Office, and integrated Finance governance. Implementation plan spans 40+ steps from Month 0 (2026-10-14) to Month 84 (2033-10-14). Escalation matrix covers 5 critical decision types. Monitoring approach specifies 6 distinct tracking methodologies. Audit procedures detail 8 compliance domains. Coverage appears comprehensive for a capital-constrained, high-ambition R&D programme.
  2. Internal Consistency Check: Logical alignment across stages is confirmed with one caveat. Implementation plan correctly references the four governance bodies and assigns step ownership. Escalation matrix identifies Scientific Steering Committee as the primary escalation point, consistent with the Stage 2 authority definitions. Monitoring plan ties KPI tracking to gate criteria defined in Stage 3 and escalates to the correct bodies. However, one inconsistency detected: the red team's authority to 'delay gate decisions up to 3 weeks' (Stage 2, red team decision_rights) does not appear explicitly in the Stage 4 escalation matrix; this creates ambiguity about whether a red-team holdback is an escalation requiring Funder sign-off or is unilaterally enforceable. Recommendation: Stage 4 should include a line for 'Red Team Holds Gate Decision for Verification,' clarifying that up to 3-week delays are red-team-executable without Steering Committee override, but >3-week delays do require escalation.
  3. Potential Gap 1—Clarity of Ultimate Project Sponsor Authority: The governance documents reference 'Project Sponsor' as the pre-existing funder authority (Stage 1, implementation plan Step 1), but do not clearly specify the Sponsor's role in the ongoing Scientific Steering Committee governance. Is the Funder representative (non-voting observer per Stage 2 Steering Committee membership) the Project Sponsor's delegate, or are they separate entities? Implementation Plan Step 1 states 'Project Sponsor confirms programme Director,' but later steps show the Director and Steering Committee making major decisions with 'Funder approval required' for thresholds >USD 2M or programme stop. Clarification needed: (i) Is 'Project Sponsor' synonymous with 'Funder'? (ii) Does the Sponsor have any unilateral halt authority, or does all stop authority flow through Steering Committee escalation to Funder? (iii) If the Sponsor is separate from Funder, what is the Sponsor's decision authority over governance changes (e.g., replacing Director, dissolving red team)?
  4. Potential Gap 2—Process Definition for Conflict of Interest and Whistleblower Investigation: While Stage 1 Audit Details specify 'conflicts of interest' as part of corruption prevention and include employee disclosure forms, the governance framework does not define a formal conflict-of-interest management process for Committee members or staff. Example gap: If a Chemistry Lead's spouse works for a precursor vendor bidding for a contract, is the Lead recused from the vendor-selection decision? Who decides? If a researcher suspects deliberate data misrepresentation by a peer (potential 'whistleblower' scenario), what is the reporting path—directly to red team, to EHS Officer, to Steering Committee, or to an external ethics hotline? Implementation Plan and Escalation Matrix are silent on these governance processes. Recommendation: Add a Governance Appendix defining (i) conflict-of-interest disclosure and recusal procedures for Steering Committee and key staff, (ii) anonymous whistleblower reporting channels (e.g., external ethics consultant hotline), (iii) investigation and remediation procedures for alleged data integrity violations or misconduct.
  5. Potential Gap 3—Delegation of Authority Below Committee Level and Coordinators' Decision Rights: The framework defines decision authority at three levels: Director (<USD 500K), Steering Committee (USD 500K–2M), Funder (>USD 2M). However, the plan involves 80–120 FTE, implying dozens of team leads and coordinators (synthesis manager, pilot-line manager, characterization manager, data engineer, lab safety coordinator, finance controller, etc.). None of these roles have explicit delegated decision authority defined. Example: If the Pilot-Line Manager discovers a critical equipment failure costing USD 50K to repair and requiring 1-week downtime, can the Manager authorize the repair or must it escalate to the Chemistry Lead and Director? If the Synthesis Manager identifies a precursor supplier shortage and needs to authorize emergency expedited shipping (+USD 10K), what is the approval path? Clarification needed: Develop decision-authority matrix for key staff roles (Synthesis Manager, Pilot-Line Manager, Characterization Manager, Lab Safety Coordinator) specifying (i) decision types within their authority, (ii) thresholds (monetary or schedule impact), (iii) escalation triggers. Suggest: Synthesis Manager approves material purchases <USD 20K and routine operations; Pilot-Line Manager approves equipment maintenance <USD 50K and day-to-day scheduling; Characterization Manager approves partner scheduling and equipment time; Lab Safety Coordinator halts any unsafe operation unilaterally, escalates within 48 hours.
  6. Potential Gap 4—Change Control and Scope-Deviation Process: The governance framework defines gates and milestone decisions but does not articulate a formal change-control process for mid-tranche scope changes or scope deviation requests. Example scenarios: At Month 20 (2028-06-14), a Chemistry Lead proposes adding a fourth active chemistry pathway (instead of three) based on promising early data from a collaboration. Or, a partner laboratory becomes unavailable and the programme must commission a new characterization facility on-site (USD 5–10M capital, 6-month build). Or, a major equipment supplier offers a significant discount if the programme doubles its order. The Escalation Matrix covers financial overruns and risk thresholds but does not specify approval workflow for mid-tranche scope additions or reductions. Recommendation: Define a Change Control Board (subset of Steering Committee: Director, Finance Manager, Chemistry Lead, red-team lead) with authority to approve scope additions <USD 5M or schedule impacts <4 weeks within current tranche; larger changes require full Steering Committee vote and Funder sign-off. Require a change-control form documenting: (i) justification, (ii) cost/schedule impact, (iii) risk assessment, (iv) approval signature.
  7. Potential Gap 5—Stakeholder Communication and Regulator Engagement Protocols: The governance documents specify that the Chief EHS Officer engages Austin Fire Authority and TCEQ (Stage 3 implementation, Month 0–1 = 2026-10-14 to 2026-11-14), and that quarterly regulator meetings are held (Stage 2 EHS Office, meeting cadence). However, the framework does not define protocols for proactive regulator communication if programme decisions might affect compliance (e.g., if a chemistry pivots to lithium-metal synthesis not previously disclosed in Phase 1 permit, or if abuse-test results reveal thermal-runaway hazards requiring permit modification). Similarly, no protocol exists for managing regulator feedback into governance decisions. Example: What if the fire authority raises a concern about dry-room humidity control that requires a USD 1–2M retrofit? Is this escalated to Steering Committee as a permitting risk, or does EHS Officer have delegated authority to approve the retrofit? Recommendation: Define Regulator Engagement Protocol (part of Stage 2 EHS Office charter) specifying: (i) quarterly standing meetings with fire authority and TCEQ (documented agenda, minutes, action items), (ii) process for notifying regulators of significant scope changes (lithium-metal synthesis, abuse-chamber commissioning, waste-stream changes), (iii) escalation trigger if regulator feedback requires >USD 1M retrofit or >4-week delay, (iv) public transparency (e.g., annual EHS public statement to community and regulators per audit procedures).

Tough Questions

  1. By Month 12 (2027-10-14), what is the probability-weighted forecast for each of the three active chemistry pathways to achieve >=500 Wh/kg and >=950 Wh/L interim threshold by the Month 18 (2028-04-14) gate? If any pathway is projected <70% likelihood of gate pass, what is the contingency timeline and cost to activate the reserve chemistry or pivot to a fourth candidate?
  2. Third-party verification at Month 30 (2029-04-14) requires >=3 independent replicates per finalist chemistry to meet >=500 Wh/kg AND >=950 Wh/L in the same cells with 90% of cells within ±10% tolerance. If in-house cell builds exhibit 15–20% Wh/kg variability (not the proposed 10%), will the programme's internal measurement methodology or pilot-line process control be deemed inadequate, forcing extended qualification before Month 30 (2029-04-14) gate? Who is responsible for reconciling in-house vs. third-party measurement discrepancies if they exceed ±5%?
  3. The budget allocation assumes payroll of USD 8–12 M/yr (70 M over 7 years) for 80–120 FTE. If competitive salary pressure from Tesla and other Austin firms forces payroll to USD 12–14 M/yr (+USD 4–6 M/yr overrun, ~USD 28–42 M cumulative), which budget categories will be compressed—characterization instruments, pilot-line capital, partner co-funding absorption, or contingency reserves? What is the attrition threshold (proposed 15%/yr) that would trigger a mandatory compensation review and reallocation decision by Month 24 (2028-10-14)?
  4. Permitting slippage of 6–8 months (plausible risk) pushes operational start from Month 3 (2027-01-14) to Month 9 (2027-07-14), reducing effective programme duration to 75–78 months. If this occurs and no contingency outsourced-synthesis agreement is pre-negotiated by Month 6 (2027-04-14), what is the recovery plan? Will the Month 18 (2028-04-14) gate be deferred to Month 24 (2028-10-14), or will chemistry selection proceed with limited or no pouch-cell data, risking non-verification until Month 60+ (2031-10-14)?
  5. The staged chemistry tournament assumes three active pathways with clear differentiation (e.g., lithium-sulfur, anode-free solid-state, conversion cathode). If by Month 12 (2027-10-14) early data shows all three pathways converging on the same electrolyte chemistry and cell-design requirements (e.g., all three benefit from identical ionic-liquid electrolyte, making them variants of one approach rather than independent hedges), does the Steering Committee have authority to collapse the three teams into one and redirect freed budget to a true reserve chemistry? Who decides and when?
  6. The 1000 Wh/L volumetric target is treated as an interim 950 Wh/L threshold at Month 30 (2029-04-14) but a hard 1000 Wh/L final requirement at Month 72 (2032-10-14). If the winning chemistry demonstrably hits >=500 Wh/kg but maxes out at 880–920 Wh/L due to fundamental separator thickness and electrolyte-volume constraints, is the programme authorized to descope the volumetric target and deliver a partial success (500+ Wh/kg, ~900 Wh/L, >=300 cycles)? What is the Steering Committee's and Funder's acceptance threshold for 'missing' one of the two headline targets?
  7. Red-team verification authority includes the right to delay gate decisions up to 3 weeks for independent validation, and to recommend chemistry deprioritization if replication fails. If at Month 36 (2029-10-14) the red team's replication results contradict the chemistry team's claimed Wh/kg by >10% (red team measures 480 Wh/kg, chemistry team claims 510 Wh/kg), and the chemistry team contests the red team's cell-build methodology or measurement calibration, how is the dispute resolved? Does the red-team finding override the chemistry-team claim (as stated in Stage 2 red-team decision_rights), or does Steering Committee arbitration occur? What is the escalation path if disagreement persists and jeopardizes the Month 36 (2029-10-14) gate decision timeline?

Summary

The governance framework for a seven-year, USD 300M battery-invention programme balances hedged chemistry risk (staged tournament with formal gates at Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14), rigorous system-level discipline (cell-level mass-and-volume model, dual energy-density thresholds from Month 12 = 2027-10-14), and pragmatic cost control (modular leased pilot line, partner co-funding, evidence-linked tranche release). Core strengths include clear Scientific Steering Committee decision authority, independent red-team verification to protect data integrity, phased permitting and EHS governance to de-risk regulatory slippage, and formal contingency planning for chemistry failure. The USD 20M reserve (inside the USD 300M cap) and USD 15M pivot runway preserve flexibility for mid-programme redirection if a leading chemistry fails by Month 30–36 (2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14). Cycle-life (>=300 cycles at 80% retention) and safety (thermal-runaway onset >=120°C) are hardened as gate criteria from Month 3 (2027-01-14) onwards, preventing descent into non-commercial dead ends. Technology transfer planning begins by Month 60 (2031-10-14) and concludes by Month 84 (2033-10-14), aligned with the non-commercial, invention-focused objective. Identified governance gaps—clarity of Project Sponsor authority, conflict-of-interest and whistleblower procedures, delegated authority for team coordinators, change-control process, and regulator communication protocol—are addressable through governance-procedure appendices without reshaping the core structure. Financial viability depends on (i) permitting not slipping >6 months, (ii) payroll not exceeding USD 12M/yr ceiling, (iii) at least one reserve chemistry pre-staged by Month 24 (2028-10-14) to enable 4–6 week pivots if two active chemistries fail, and (iv) partner cost-sharing sustaining >=15% of shared costs. The framework is fit-for-purpose for a capital-constrained, high-ambition, 84-month invention programme with strong emphasis on early risk identification, independent validation, and preserving optionality through formal gates.

Suggestion 1 - Battery500 Consortium (US DOE, led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory)

DOE Vehicle Technologies Office programme launched in 2016 to reach 500 Wh/kg lithium-metal pouch cells with 1,000 cycles at the cell level. Multi-university and national-lab consortium with a phase structure and a shared cell-fabrication and testing capability. Renewed for a second phase. Focused on lithium-metal anodes with high-nickel cathodes, electrolytes and cell engineering.

Success Metrics

Reported pouch cells at roughly 350-500 Wh/kg-class levels with limited cycle life (approximate, not verified) Publication output and patents across partner institutions Standardized pouch-cell protocols used for cross-team comparison

Risks and Challenges Faced

Cycle life collapse at high energy density: addressed via electrolyte and pressure-engineering research and a cell-level test standard. Material-level numbers not transferring to cells: mitigated by common pouch-cell fabrication at the lead lab. Coordination across many institutions: managed by a central leadership and thrust-area structure.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.battery500.org https://www.energy.gov/eere/vehicles/battery-500-consortium

Actionable Steps

Contact the Battery500 consortium leadership via the website contact form (PNNL programme office). Ask the PNNL battery group for cell-build protocol and pouch-cell metrics documentation. Approach the DOE Vehicle Technologies Office battery R&D programme managers about gate design lessons.

Rationale for Suggestion

Closest public analogue: same 500 Wh/kg cell-level target, pouch-cell proof standard and consortium partnering model. Lessons on cycle-life gates and shared fabrication directly inform the staged tournament and cycle-life threshold. Geographically distant (Washington State) but US-based.

Suggestion 2 - Sion Power Licerion lithium-metal cell development (Tucson, Arizona)

Tucson-based company developing protected lithium-metal anode cells (Licerion) with lithium-sulfur heritage, targeting very high gravimetric energy density, with US DOE and other funding and a pilot-scale line. Demonstrates a layered protective-interface approach similar to the hybrid interlayer concept.

Success Metrics

Publicly claimed cell energy density in the 400+ Wh/kg class (approximate, not verified) Operation of a pilot line in Tucson Multi-year development programme with customer and government funding

Risks and Challenges Faced

Lithium dendrites and cycle life: mitigated through protective layer engineering. Scaling from lab to pilot: addressed via a dedicated pilot production line. Balancing energy density with cycle life across applications: managed by segmenting target markets.

Where to Find More Information

https://sionpower.com Company press releases and DOE ARPA-E / VTO project listings

Actionable Steps

Contact Sion Power business development through the company website. Request a technical briefing on protected lithium interface design and pilot-line lessons. Explore a licensing or evaluation discussion through the corporate contact channel.

Rationale for Suggestion

Southwest US organization with Li-S and lithium-metal heritage and a pilot line; a practical template for interface protection, pilot scaling and licensing-oriented operation. Limited public detail on cycle data, so verify claims directly.

Suggestion 3 - Solid Power sulfide solid-electrolyte pilot programme (Colorado)

Colorado-based developer of sulfide solid electrolytes and all-solid-state cells, operating a pilot cell line and electrolyte production line, with automaker development partnerships (BMW, Ford) and a licensing-oriented model for cell designs and electrolyte supply.

Success Metrics

Operating pilot electrolyte and cell lines (documented in company filings) Automaker joint development agreements Delivery of A-sample cells to partners for validation

Risks and Challenges Faced

Dry-room and sulfide handling: addressed with dedicated dry-room line. Stack-pressure and interface resistance: tackled via cell design and partner validation. Path to commercialization without owning mass production: pursued through licensing and partner-manufacturing.

Where to Find More Information

https://solidpowerbattery.com SEC filings and investor presentations (company site)

Actionable Steps

Contact the investor relations or business development team via the company site. Request a discussion on pilot-line sizing and dry-room design. Ask about licensing terms and technology-transfer structure.

Rationale for Suggestion

Mirrors the anode-free/solid-state tournament entry and the invent-then-license model. Provides pilot-line and dry-room cost and timeline references, and a US-based licensing precedent.

Suggestion 4 - Secondary: UT Austin Texas Materials Institute / Goodenough-lineage battery research

University of Texas at Austin battery materials research groups with solid-state and lithium-metal expertise and shared characterization facilities, located in the programme's own city.

Success Metrics

Publication record in solid-state and lithium-metal materials (not verified in detail) Availability of shared characterization facilities

Risks and Challenges Faced
