Create Document 1: Project Charter and Goals Statement

ID: 370f82e7-9a5e-4910-8409-b2402d41dec3

Description: Formal charter defining the programme goal (invent a >=500 Wh/kg and >=1000 Wh/L cell at cell level, third-party verified, licensable), success criteria (300 cycles at 80% retention, thermal-runaway onset >=120°C), timeline (84 months, Month 0 = 2026-10-14 to Month 84 = 2033-10-14), budget (USD 300 M fixed cap), and governance. Primary audience: Steering Committee, funder, external stakeholders. Approvals: Funder, Steering Committee.

Responsible Role Type: Programme Director

Primary Template: PMI Project Charter Template

Secondary Template: World Bank Logical Framework

Steps to Create:

  • Reconcile user constraints (500 Wh/kg, 1000 Wh/L, USD 300 M, 84 months, Austin location) with the selected Pragmatic Foundation strategy.
  • Define SMART success criteria: >=500 Wh/kg, >=1000 Wh/L, >=300 cycles at 80% retention, thermal-runaway onset >=120°C, third-party verified, reproducibility >=90% within ±10%.
  • Document dependencies: site lease and permitting, partner agreements, clean-room onboarding, gate decision protocols.
  • Identify key risks and mitigation (chemistry failure, volumetric shortfall, permitting slip, payroll overrun, pivot cost).
  • Obtain signed approval from Funder and Steering Committee by Month 1 (2026-11-14).

Approval Authorities: Funder, Programme Director, Steering Committee chair

Essential Information:

  • Define the three formal gates (Month 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14) with explicit pass/fail thresholds for each chemistry candidate: Wh/kg ≥500, Wh/L ≥950 (interim) and ≥1000 (final), cycle life ≥300 cycles at 80%, thermal-runaway onset ≥120°C, and reproducibility ≥90% within ±10%.
  • Document the Scientific Steering Committee's decision authority and timeline: gate reviews conclude within 3 weeks; advancement, descope, or pivot decisions are made and communicated by a named decision authority (proposed: Programme Director with Steering Committee consensus or funder tiebreak).
  • Specify the go/no-go rules at each gate: Month 18 (2028-04-14) advances 2–3 chemistries if projected cell-level targets are met; Month 30 (2029-04-14) requires third-party verified pouch-cell data showing both Wh/kg and Wh/L; Month 36 (2029-10-14) selects one finalist or triggers a stop/descope decision if no chemistry meets thresholds.
  • Establish the deprioritization and fallback rules: candidates with <250 cycles at 80% are deprioritized from Month 24 (2028-10-14) unless within one 2–4 month redesign; volumetric shortfall triggers a 6-month architecture sprint by Month 30 (2029-04-14); a failed Month 36 (2029-10-14) gate activates the pre-staged reserve chemistry (Month 36–42 = 2029-10-14 to 2030-04-14) or halts T4 funding release (USD 90 M) pending descope.
  • Detail the data and evidence requirements for gate passage: Month 18 (2028-04-14) requires simulated and coin-cell cycle data plus safety screening; Month 30 (2029-04-14) requires independent third-party pouch-cell measurement (≥100 mAh capacity, ≥3 replicates per chemistry); Month 36 (2029-10-14) requires the same pouch data plus abuse testing (thermal runaway, nail penetration, overcharge) and manufacturing reproducibility (batch-to-batch ±10%).
  • Document the red team's (independent verification group) role: 2–3 external scientists replicate top-performing results, challenge progress claims and recommend go/no-go; red team authority is advisory to Steering Committee, not veto; replication criteria and timeline (within 2–4 weeks of claimed result) are specified.
  • Specify the financial and timeline consequences of each decision outcome: advancing all 3 chemistries costs +USD 5–10 M/yr (estimate); pivoting to reserve chemistry costs USD 5–10 M and 6–10 months (estimate) versus pre-staged reserve (4–6 weeks); stopping or descoping releases a contingency blueprint for a simplified target (e.g., 480 Wh/kg, skip 1000 Wh/L, or extend timeline to Month 96 = 2034-10-14 with revised budget).
  • Create a gate-review meeting template and checklist: attendees (Steering Committee, red team, chemistry leads, funder rep), pre-meeting data package (candidate rankings, Wh/kg/Wh/L/cycle-life summary, third-party test reports if applicable), decision agenda (pass/fail per candidate, advance/deprioritize/eliminate rules, funding implications, risk flags), and post-meeting communication (decision memo, timeline update, budget adjustment).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous gate criteria allow a chemistry to advance despite falling short (e.g., 480 Wh/kg claimed but third-party test shows 460), wasting USD 5–15 M and 6–12 months on a non-viable path.
  • Unclear decision authority at gates causes 4–8 week delays (Risk #13) while Steering Committee, funder and Programme Director debate who has final say, compressing post-gate timelines and forcing rushed pivots.
  • Missing deprioritization rules allow candidates with <200 cycle life to remain in the tournament, consuming resources that should shift to more promising chemistries; late discovery of poor cycle life at Month 48–60 (2030-10-14 to 2031-10-14) forces late-stage redesign at USD 10–20 M cost (estimate) with insufficient runway.
  • Lack of volumetric-density gate criteria allows Wh/kg focus to dominate; a chemistry hitting 520 Wh/kg but only 800 Wh/L due to thick separators is discovered only at Month 36–48 (2029-10-14 to 2030-10-14), requiring a 6–12 month architecture sprint that compresses final optimization or forces partial success.
  • Red team authority is undefined: if replication attempts fail to confirm a claimed result but authority is unclear, dispute resolution delays gate decision by 2–4 weeks and creates team friction; alternatively, red team is ignored and credibility of the final result suffers.
  • Absence of a stop/descope rule at Month 36 (2029-10-14) allows the programme to continue funding all remaining candidates despite none meeting thresholds, burning USD 90 M (T4) on a failing path instead of pivoting or winding down gracefully.
  • Missing third-party verification requirements at gates allow in-house claimed numbers to differ from independent lab measurements, discovered only at final validation (Month 72 = 2032-10-14), threatening patent value and licensing appeal by 30–50% (estimate) and delaying commercialization by 12–24 months.

Worst Case Scenario: A chemistry advances at Month 18 (2028-04-14) with promising coin-cell data but no pouch-cell verification. By Month 30 (2029-04-14), third-party testing reveals measured Wh/kg of 460 (not 500), cycle life of 180 cycles (not 300), and Wh/L of 820 (not 950). The gate passes under loose criteria, consuming USD 10–15 M in Months 24–30 (2028-10-14 to 2029-04-14). At Month 36 (2029-10-14), the chemistry still does not meet targets; no clear stop rule exists. The Steering Committee splits on descope; decision is deferred 6 weeks while the funder and Programme Director debate. By Month 42 (2030-04-14), the programme pivots to the reserve chemistry (unprepared, costing 8–10 months). First cells from the reserve are ready at Month 50–52 (2031-04-14 to 2031-06-14). With only 31–34 months remaining, proof-of-concept is achieved but with insufficient time for 500+ cycle life confirmation, abuse testing or third-party verification. The final result is a cell demonstrated at 480 Wh/kg, 850 Wh/L, 280 cycles—below stated targets—and without independent verification. Patent value drops 40–50%; licensing is delayed 18–24 months; the USD 300 M investment is judged a partial failure despite technical effort.

Best Case Scenario: Clear gate criteria and decision authority enable Month 18 (2028-04-14) review to advance two strong chemistries (lithium-sulfur, anode-free solid-state) and deprioritize one (conversion cathode with low projected cycle life). By Month 24 (2028-10-14), the pre-staged reserve chemistry (fourth option) is prepared. At Month 30 (2029-04-14), third-party pouch testing confirms one chemistry (anode-free solid-state) meets all thresholds: 510 Wh/kg, 980 Wh/L, 320 cycles, thermal runaway onset 135°C. The red team replicates the result within 4 weeks, confirming credibility. Gate decision is made within 3 weeks; the Steering Committee recommends advancing the anode-free candidate to optimization and descoping the lithium-sulfur path. Funding for Months 36–84 (2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14) proceeds with T4 (USD 90 M) released on schedule. Months 36–72 (2029-10-14 to 2032-10-14) focus on cycle-life improvement, manufacturing scale-up and abuse-testing maturation. By Month 72 (2032-10-14), independent third-party testing confirms final cell: 515 Wh/kg, 1020 Wh/L, 380 cycles at 80%, thermal runaway onset 140°C. Reproducibility across 50 cells: 92% within ±10%. Patent estate includes five provisional filings on compositions, electrolyte architectures and cell formats. Licensing framework is negotiated with two prospective manufacturers by Month 60 (2031-10-14); exclusive license signed by Month 80 (2033-06-14). Programme delivers on time, within budget and with a defensible, licensable invention.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If formalizing three separate gates is too resource-intensive, consolidate to a single comprehensive gate at Month 30 (2029-04-14) with rigorous third-party data, and use Months 0–30 (2026-10-14 to 2029-04-14) for rapid parallel testing to accumulate evidence. This trades earlier filtering for simpler governance but increases the risk of pursuing a failing chemistry too far.
  • If assembling an independent red team is impractical (insufficient Austin-area experts available), delegate red-team functions to a named external advisory board member (e.g., a senior battery researcher at a partner university) with formal authority to review and challenge results. Conduct replications remotely or at partner laboratories, documented via video call and written report.
  • If Steering Committee consensus cannot be achieved within 3 weeks at a gate, implement a pre-agreed tiebreak rule: funder representative casts the deciding vote after listening to debate. Document the tiebreak rule in the charter to avoid end-of-gate paralysis.
  • If third-party pouch-cell testing at Month 30 (2029-04-14) is delayed or infeasible, conduct an interim verification using a trusted partner laboratory (e.g., national laboratory with no commercial stake) as a proxy for independence. Require the partner to sign a verification and non-disclosure agreement; publish the partner's methods and results alongside in-house data to establish credibility.
  • If Month 36 (2029-10-14) gate decision triggers a stop/descope and the Steering Committee cannot agree on next steps within 6 weeks, activate a pre-agreed technical-advisory panel (three external senior battery scientists, identified and pre-committed by Month 12 = 2027-10-14) to recommend a path forward (pivot, extend timeline, reduce targets, or close). The funder accepts the panel's recommendation or formally disputes it in writing within 2 weeks.
  • If the reserve chemistry is not pre-staged by Month 24 (2028-10-14) due to budget constraints, and Month 36 (2029-10-14) gate requires a pivot, shift to a 6–12 month 'technology acquisition or partnership' phase: licence a promising chemistry from a university or battery start-up, fast-track it into the programme's cell-level framework, and resume optimization. This trades programme autonomy for speed but adds cost (USD 2–5 M license or equity stake, estimate) and IP complexity.

Create Document 2: Chemistry Pathway Tournament Strategy and Gate Criteria

ID: 5030ccde-788b-4034-b8f6-3da583b5db08

Description: Detailed strategy for staged tournament across 3 active chemistries (lithium-sulfur, anode-free solid-state, conversion cathode) plus 1 pre-staged reserve. Specifies chemistry selection criteria, go/no-go gates (Months 18, 30, 36 = 2028-04-14, 2029-04-14, 2029-10-14), quantitative success thresholds (>=500 Wh/kg material-level, >=950 Wh/L interim, >=300 cycles, >=120°C thermal onset), deprioritization rules, and pivot contingency. Primary audience: chemistry leads, Steering Committee.

Responsible Role Type: Chemistry Pathway Lead (or Lead Chemistry Team)

Primary Template: Stage-Gate Innovation Process (Cooper, IRI model)

Secondary Template: None

Steps to Create:

  • Define the three active chemistries: anode, cathode, electrolyte specification for each.
  • Document projected cell-level Wh/kg and Wh/L for each (using the mass-and-volume model, due Month 4 = 2027-02-14).
  • Specify quantitative go/no-go criteria at Months 18 (2028-04-14), 30 (2029-04-14), 36 (2029-10-14).
  • Define deprioritization rules: candidates with <250 cycles at 80% by Month 12 (2027-10-14) receive no new builds for 4 weeks pending a focused 2-4 month redesign sprint, with decision point at Month 15 (2028-01-14) or Month 18 (2028-04-14).
  • Detail reserve-chemistry specification, precursor suppliers (>=2 per material), lead times and pivot timeline (4-6 weeks execution if triggered at Month 30 = 2029-04-14).
  • Lock criteria by Month 3 (2027-01-14) via Steering Committee signed agreement attached to tranche-release conditions.

Approval Authorities: Chemistry Pathway Lead, Steering Committee, Programme Director

Essential Information:

  • Define the three active chemistries in the tournament: specify anode, cathode, electrolyte and catholyte pairing for each (e.g., Li-metal + Ni/rich-oxide + liquid HCC; Li-S + ?; anode-free solid-state + halide), with material-level projected Wh/kg and Wh/L for each derived from the mass-and-volume model (due Month 4 = 2027-02-14).
  • Quantify go/no-go success criteria at each gate: Month 18 (2028-04-14) [projected cell Wh/kg ≥500, interim Wh/L ≥950, cycle data, safety ranking]; Month 30 (2029-04-14) [third-party measured pouch cells meeting ≥500 Wh/kg AND ≥950 Wh/L in same cells, ≥300 cycles at 80% retention, 90% within ±10% reproducibility]; Month 36 (2029-10-14) [finalists meeting Month 30 (2029-04-14) thresholds plus thermal-runaway onset ≥120°C].
  • Detail deprioritization and re-prioritization rules: candidates falling below 250 cycles at 80% by Month 12 (2027-10-14) (measured data, not projected) are paused from new builds for 4 weeks pending focused 2-4 month redesign; decision point Month 15 or 18 (2028-01-14, 2028-04-14); candidates not advancing by Month 24 (2028-10-14) are archived unless within one redesign sprint.
  • Specify the pre-staged reserve chemistry: identify composition, precursor suppliers (≥2 per material with dual-sourced qualification), lead times (estimated 8-12 weeks for key materials), pilot-line equipment reconfiguration needs, and staff cross-training plan (20-30% of synthesis and pilot team trained by Month 12 = 2027-10-14).
  • Articulate pivot-contingency mechanics: trigger decision at Month 30 (2029-04-14) or Month 36 (2029-10-14); if two of three active chemistries fail, reserve is pre-staged (materials on order by Month 24 = 2028-10-14); pivot execution target ≤6 weeks, reaching first pouch builds ~Month 42-43 (2030-04-14).
  • Document gate decision-making authority: Steering Committee (director, chemistry leads, external advisor, funder representative) has explicit sign-off; decision timeline ≤3 weeks per gate; red-team (2-3 scientists) provides independent result verification before Steering Committee review.
  • Lock all criteria and deprioritization thresholds by Month 3 (2027-01-14) via formal Steering Committee agreement attached to T2 (USD 80 M) release conditions at Month 12 (2027-10-14); any criterion change requires Steering Committee and funder approval.
  • Identify deprioritization thresholds that do NOT result in full abandonment: chemistry < 250 cycles → 4-week pause + 2-4 month redesign window; chemistry with <950 Wh/L projected → flagged for architecture sprint before Month 36 (2029-10-14) gate; chemistry with thermal onset <100°C → lower priority but not eliminated until Month 24 (2028-10-14) decision.
  • Articulate success metrics that are system-level (cell Wh/kg and Wh/L, not material-level values alone) and tie to the Reference Application Anchor duty profile (rate, temperature, cycle life, form factor) from Month 12 (2027-10-14) onward.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Vague or missing go/no-go thresholds leave gate decisions subjective; Steering Committee and funder argue over what 'viable' means at Month 30 (2029-04-14), delaying decision 4-8 weeks and compressing the post-gate optimization window from 48 months to 40-44 months.
  • Undefined deprioritization rules allow underperforming chemistries to consume budget and pilot-line throughput through Month 24 (2028-10-14) without clear stop points; wasted builds and supplies on a chemistry that will not meet 300-cycle target could cost USD 5-10 M and delay identification of viable path.
  • Missing reserve-chemistry specification and pre-staging plan means a pivot triggered at Month 30-36 (2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14) takes 6-10 months instead of ≤6 weeks; first cells with new chemistry not ready until Month 42-46 (2030-04-14 to 2030-08-14), leaving only 38-42 months for proof—insufficient for novel chemistry maturation and abuse testing.
  • Unclear pivot-cost contingency (which budget line covers re-sourcing, equipment reconfiguration, staff retraining?) forces ad hoc spending decisions; if pivot costs USD 8-15 M and reserves are exhausted elsewhere, programme either defers other work (characterization, third-party testing) or overruns the USD 20 M reserve, cutting into general contingency.
  • Absence of deprioritization triggers for cycle-life and volumetric penalties allows chemistries with subtle failure modes (dendrite growth at 250 cycles, expansion eroding 100 Wh/L) to advance past Month 18-24 (2028-04-14 to 2028-10-14) gates, only to fail at Month 30 (2029-04-14) third-party verification; USD 10-20 M in prior work becomes sunk cost.
  • Weak or absent red-team role in gate verification allows optimistic internal reports to advance weak chemistries; independent verification only at Month 30 (2029-04-14) is too late to correct Month 18 (2028-04-14) decisions, compressing the pivot window before Month 36 (2029-10-14).
  • No explicit link between gate thresholds and the duty-profile anchor (rate, temperature, cycle count) risks optimizing for 'any cell that reaches 500 Wh/kg' rather than 'a cell that can serve the stated application'; a cell that meets gravimetric target but cannot discharge at required C-rate or temperature passes gate criteria but is unusable.

Worst Case Scenario: At Month 36 (2029-10-14), all three active chemistries fail to meet month 30 (2029-04-14) thresholds—two hit <300 cycles at 80% despite 24 months of redesign, one reaches 520 Wh/kg but only 780 Wh/L due to separator thickness. With no reserve pre-staged and no clear pivot plan, the Steering Committee spends 6-8 weeks debating whether to continue or descope. A decision at Month 39-40 (2030-01-14 to 2030-02-14) to pivot to reserve chemistry means first pouch cells ~Month 48-52 (2030-10-14 to 2031-02-14), leaving 32-36 months for proof. Programme delivers coin-cell or early pouch data but cannot complete third-party verification of ≥300 cycles at ≥1000 Wh/L by Month 72 (2032-10-14); technology transfer is postponed, licensing is deferred, and the USD 300 M invention is incomplete. Alternatively, if deprioritization thresholds are absent, chemistries consume budget through month 60 (2031-10-14) before cycle-life and volumetric failures are discovered; programme runs short of funds for final optimization and third-party verification, missing Month 84 (2033-10-14) delivery.

Best Case Scenario: Clear, quantified go/no-go criteria are locked by Month 3 (2027-01-14) and published to the team. Chemistry A reaches Month 18 (2028-04-14) targets; by Month 24 (2028-10-14) it demonstrates 310 cycles at 80%, hitting 510 Wh/kg. Chemistry B falls short at Month 18 (2028-04-14) on Wh/L and is deprioritized (no new builds for 4 weeks); redesign during Months 20-24 (2028-06-14 to 2028-10-14) adds a thinner separator and increases density to 960 Wh/L interim projection. Month 30 (2029-04-14) third-party verification confirms Chemistry A at 505 Wh/kg, 1010 Wh/L, 305 cycles at 80%, 92% within ±10%. Month 36 (2029-10-14) gate selects Chemistry A; reserve is stood down. Months 36-72 (2029-10-14 to 2032-10-14) focus on reproducibility, abuse testing, cycle-life extension to 500+ cycles and technology-transfer design. Month 72 (2032-10-14) final pouch cell verified by third party: 505 Wh/kg, 1020 Wh/L, 310 cycles at 80%, onset 125°C. Month 84 (2033-10-14) delivery includes process documentation, pilot-scale demonstration and a signed licensing agreement with a manufacturer. Clear criteria enable Steering Committee to make rapid decisions, avoid funding dead-end chemistries, and compress the pivot timeline if needed, maximizing confidence in the final result and its licensing appeal.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the three active chemistries cannot be fully specified by Month 2 (2026-12-14), defer detailed go/no-go thresholds to Month 6 (2027-04-14) after initial small-scale (coin-cell) data are collected, but require that all quantitative criteria (cycle-life, Wh/L, thermal onset) are set and approved by Scientific Steering Committee no later than Month 9 (2027-07-14), with formal announcement to all teams and funders by Month 10 (2027-08-14). This delays gate clarity by 3 months but avoids specifying criteria for chemistries that have not yet been initiated.
  • If reserve-chemistry pre-staging cannot be completed by Month 24 (2028-10-14) due to supply or staffing constraints, execute a 'pivot-readiness checkpoint' at Month 27 (2029-01-14): place orders for reserve precursors, identify equipment reconfiguration steps, and conduct a 1-week dry-run pilot-line changeover simulation. This shortens execution time from 6-10 months to 6-8 weeks and allows a Month 30 (2029-04-14) decision to translate into Month 31-32 (2029-05-14 to 2029-06-14) commissioning. Cost: USD 300-500 K for simulation and pre-ordered materials; benefit is compressed pivot timeline.
  • If the Steering Committee cannot reach consensus within 3 weeks at a gate decision, escalate to an external technical arbitrator (e.g., National Academies or national laboratory battery-science panel, pre-identified at Month 6 = 2027-04-14) who provides a non-binding recommendation within 5 days. Committee then has 2 additional weeks to decide, capping total gate-decision time at 5 weeks instead of 3-8 weeks (or indefinite deadlock). Cost: USD 20-50 K per arbitration; benefit is schedule certainty and reduced dispute.
  • If the red-team verification at Month 30 (2029-04-14) reveals data discrepancies (internal claims of 310 cycles vs. independent replication showing 290), and Chemistry A is at risk of failing the gate, allow Chemistry B (which passed Month 18 = 2028-04-14 but was deprioritized) to be rapidly re-evaluated. If B achieved 300+ cycles during its redesign window (Months 20-24 = 2028-06-14 to 2028-10-14) and meets Wh/L target, advance B to Month 30-36 (2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14) verification in parallel with Chemistry A. This hedges against red-team findings and avoids a full pivot, at cost of parallel verification (USD 2-4 M additional third-party testing).
  • If governance deadlock or funding constraints prevent the Mass-and-Volume Model from being live and updated quarterly, establish a simpler, 'fit-for-gate' spreadsheet model by Month 6 (2027-04-14) that projects cell Wh/kg and Wh/L from material composition and known density/mass rules-of-thumb. While less accurate than a full engineering model, it is sufficient to flag chemistries that obviously cannot meet Wh/L targets (e.g., thick-separator chemistries) and to decide deprioritization by Month 12 (2027-10-14). Upgrade to full model Months 12-24 (2027-10-14 to 2028-10-14) if time and resources allow. Cost: minimal; benefit is early warning without full model build-out.

Create Document 3: Cell-Level Mass-and-Volume Model and Packaging Penalty Analysis

ID: 87804d32-c8e2-4003-b17c-d3f38f788115

Description: Live parametric model that back-calculates material-level Wh/kg and Wh/L targets from the cell-level goals (>=500 Wh/kg, >=1000 Wh/L). Accounts for current collectors (10-20 µm), separator (25-30 µm, chemistry-specific), electrolyte volume (0.5-1.5 mL/Ah), pouch laminate (300-400 µm) and pressure hardware. Includes time-dependent swelling projections (sulfur +25% volume, anode-free >=50% anode thickness per cycle). Quarterly updates with variance analysis (>10% gaps flagged for investigation). Primary audience: chemistry leads, cell engineering, Steering Committee.

Responsible Role Type: Cell Engineering Lead

Primary Template: Custom parametric design spreadsheet or simulation code (MATLAB, Python)

Secondary Template: None

Steps to Create:

  • Collect baseline data: current-collector foil thickness, separator porosity, electrolyte fill fraction, pouch material mass per cm² from published benchmarks and supplier specs.
  • Define chemistry-specific swelling assumptions: lithium-sulfur cathode volume change, anode-free stack-height growth per cycle, separator compression under pressure.
  • Build the model: (cell Wh/kg target) = (material Wh/kg) × (active-material mass fraction) / (total cell mass including inactive); iterate for Wh/L.
  • Project cell-level Wh/L for all three candidates by Month 6 (2027-04-14); flag any <950 Wh/L despite >500 Wh/kg material performance for targeted separator/electrolyte-volume redesign.
  • Publish quarterly updates with reconciliation against actual pouch-cell measured data; investigate and document any >10% discrepancy.
  • Finalize and lock model assumptions by Month 3 (2027-01-14) via Steering Committee approval.

Approval Authorities: Cell Engineering Lead, Steering Committee

Essential Information:

  • Parametric model translating cell-level targets (≥500 Wh/kg, ≥1000 Wh/L, ≥300 cycles at 80% retention) into required material-level energy density by accounting for inactive-mass components: current collectors (10–20 µm), separator (25–30 µm, chemistry-specific), electrolyte volume (0.5–1.5 mL/Ah), pouch laminate (300–400 µm), pressure hardware and time-dependent swelling (sulfur +25% volume per cycle; anode-free ≥50% anode thickness per cycle).
  • Quarterly reconciliation of model projections against measured pouch-cell data; investigation and documentation of any discrepancy exceeding ±10%, with root-cause and design response.
  • Chemistry-specific sub-models: separate Wh/kg and Wh/L calculations for lithium-sulfur, anode-free solid-state and conversion-cathode chemistries, including separator and electrolyte-volume trade-offs that erode volumetric density.
  • Flag mechanism: identify any candidate chemistry projecting <950 Wh/L (interim threshold, proposed) despite ≥500 Wh/kg material performance, triggering targeted separator/electrolyte redesign or deprioritization by Month 18 (2028-04-14).
  • Live updates locked by Month 3 (2027-01-14) via Steering Committee approval; model assumptions (swelling rates, electrolyte density, current-collector thickness) documented and justified against published benchmarks or supplier data.
  • Variance-analysis dashboard: track which inactive-mass component dominates Wh/kg loss (e.g., separator thickness versus pouch laminate weight) so design effort targets the highest-impact lever.
  • Integration with gate criteria: model output (projected cell-level Wh/kg and Wh/L) feeds directly into Month 18 (2028-04-14), Month 30 (2029-04-14) and Month 36 (2029-10-14) go/no-go decisions.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate or outdated model allows chemistry candidates to advance on material-level Wh/kg claims while cell-level Wh/L remains unachievable; discovered late (Month 48–60 = 2030-10-14 to 2031-10-14), forces 6–12 month architecture redesign or acceptance of partial success, consuming USD 8–15 M (estimate) and compressing final optimization window by 12–24 months.
  • Missing or understated swelling projections mean separator and electrolyte-volume penalties emerge only after pouch cells are built and cycled; lithium-sulfur and anode-free candidates may reach ≥500 Wh/kg but fall short of ≥1000 Wh/L, forcing late architecture pivots or reducing invention value by 30–40% for licensing.
  • Unexplained ±10% or larger discrepancies between model and measured data (overstating material-level target achievability or hidden packaging losses) erode Steering Committee confidence in gate decisions; unclear variance analysis delays identification of failed chemistries by 6–8 weeks per cycle, compressing the chemistry tournament timeline.
  • Model locked without Steering Committee sign-off by Month 3 (2027-01-14) allows inconsistent assumptions across the three chemistry tracks; candidates judged against different inactive-mass baselines introduce bias or false comparisons.
  • Lack of quarterly updates or frozen assumptions mean changes in separator supplier, electrolyte fill strategy or pouch laminate sourcing are not reflected; decisions based on outdated mass/volume predictions waste months on technically unachievable targets.

Worst Case Scenario: Model is built late (Month 8–10 = 2027-06-14 to 2027-08-14) or with unvalidated assumptions, and is not reconciled against actual pouch-cell data until Month 36 (2029-10-14) chemistry-selection gate. At that time, it emerges that a leading chemistry achieves 520 Wh/kg but only 850 Wh/L due to thick separators and large electrolyte volume not captured in earlier material-level screening. A second chemistry similarly underperforms on volumetric density. The third candidate meets both targets but has cycle life <250 cycles. Steering Committee faces a choice: spend 6–12 months redesigning all three chemistries (consuming USD 8–15 M and compressing final proof window to 36–42 months), or accept a lower-ambition result (500 Wh/kg but 850 Wh/L, or ≥500 Wh/kg with <250 cycles). Programme delivers partial invention or incomplete validation, reducing licensing appeal by 30–50% and delaying commercialization by 12–24 months.

Best Case Scenario: Model is live by Month 4 (2027-02-14), validated against supplier datasheets and published benchmarks, and locked by Steering Committee by Month 3 (2027-01-14). Quarterly updates with ≤5% discrepancy against measured pouch-cell data allow rapid diagnosis of packaging inefficiencies (e.g., 'separator is consuming 8% of gravimetric target; anode-free swelling erodes volumetric density by 12%'). By Month 18 (2028-04-14), model-informed insights have guided all three chemistry teams to parallel-path solutions (thinner separators, optimized electrolyte volume, architecture variants). Month 30 (2029-04-14) verification shows all three finalists achieve ≥500 Wh/kg and ≥950 Wh/L simultaneously, and cycle-life data confirms ≥300 cycles. Steering Committee selects with confidence at Month 36 (2029-10-14), and Months 36–84 (2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14) focus purely on optimization and reliability rather than fundamental feasibility unknowns.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If full parametric model (accounting for swelling, electrolyte volume and current-collector overhead) is not feasible by Month 3 (2027-01-14), build a simplified 'mass-accounting spreadsheet' by Month 6 (2027-04-14) that tracks pouch-cell mass and volume by component and calculates Wh/kg and Wh/L from actual builds; defer detailed swelling projections until Month 12 (2027-10-14) when candidate chemistries are stabilizing.
  • If Steering Committee approval process for model assumptions is slow, schedule a rapid technical review workshop (Month 2 = 2026-12-14) with chemistry leads to align on baseline inactive-mass values (separator porosity, electrolyte density, pouch thickness) in one session; document assumptions as meeting minutes and lock within 2 weeks.

  • Incomplete month-by-month cash-flow model fails to expose gaps between planned burn and available tranche, forcing mid-year or mid-gate budget crises (e.g., payroll cannot be met in Month 20 = 2028-06-14 because opex was underestimated and no carryover reserve was reserved).

  • Unclear decision authority or sign-off timelines (e.g., who decides if T2 conditions are met?) causes 2-4 week delays at gate decisions, compressing post-gate work and allowing undeclared gate failures to slip past the decision point (e.g., 'Phase 1 permit not yet approved' discovered after T2 funding has been obligated).
  • Vague contingency-drawdown rules allow accidental or unchecked spending from the pivot runway, depleting the USD 15 M buffer before Month 36 (2029-10-14) for non-pivotal needs, leaving no runway when the actual pivot decision is made.
  • Absence of quarterly reforecasting process and update discipline allows assumptions (e.g., partner cost-sharing, equipment lead times, FTE costs) to drift without visibility, so by Month 20 (2028-06-14) actual payroll is known to be USD 14 M/yr but the tranche schedule is unchanged, forcing backdoor cuts.

Worst Case Scenario: A critical opex-versus-tranche gap (USD ~41 M shortfall in Months 36-84 = 2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14 vs. planned Months 36-84 = 2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14 tranche of USD 90 M) combined with ambiguous gate conditions and missing cash-flow discipline creates a USD 20-30 M mid-programme funding shortfall. Phase 1 permits slip 6 months, pushing T2 release from Month 12 (2027-10-14) to Month 18 (2028-04-14), yet payroll obligations for the core team (USD 10 M/yr baseline) continue, burning the Month 0-12 (2026-10-14 to 2027-10-14) tranche reserves. At Month 24 (2028-10-14), T3 gate conditions are unclear (was Month 18 = 2028-04-14 go/no-go data required, or just submitted?), delaying the USD 70 M T3 release by 6-8 weeks into Month 28 (2029-02-14). By Month 30 (2029-04-14), the Month 24-36 (2028-10-14 to 2029-10-14) tranche of USD 70 M is exhausted by payroll, pilot-line commissioning overruns, and third-party pouch-cell testing; chemistry tournament has three candidates with incomplete cycle-life and volumetric data, but USD 15 M pivot runway is needed for pre-staging the reserve chemistry if two fail. No explicit contingency drawdown authority exists, so Steering Committee is deadlocked for 2-3 weeks on whether to release pivot funds or defer work. Result: technology transfer schedule compresses by 3-4 months, final cell verification is rushed or incomplete, licensing readiness is jeopardized, and a successful 500 Wh/kg chemistry demonstration may arrive at Month 72-78 (2032-07-14 to 2033-01-14) instead of Month 72 (2032-10-14), reducing commercialization window and competitive value of the invention.

Best Case Scenario: A clear, detailed funding release schedule with explicit gate conditions, quarterly reforecasting discipline and variance thresholds enables accurate tracking of burn rate and early detection of cost or timeline risks. Month 12 (2027-10-14) T2 release proceeds on schedule after Phase 1 permit approval and signed partner agreements, unlocking USD 80 M for pilot-line commissioning and scaled-up cell builds. Month 18 (2028-04-14) go/no-go data is submitted by all three chemistry teams, red-team verification confirms cell-level projections (≥500 Wh/kg, ≥950 Wh/L, ≥300 cycle targets are plausible), and Steering Committee advances all three to the Month 24 (2028-10-14) decision point. Quarterly reforecasting at Month 15 (2028-01-14) reveals that payroll will likely reach USD 11.5 M/yr (due to necessary senior hires in interface engineering), and partner co-funding is confirmed at USD 1.2 M/yr, allowing the Finance Manager to adjust Month 24-36 (2028-10-14 to 2029-10-14) allocations to preserve the USD 15 M pivot runway. Month 30 (2029-04-14) third-party pouch-cell verification data arrives on schedule, showing two chemistries meeting both Wh/kg and volumetric thresholds and one narrowly missing volumetric by 30 Wh/L. Steering Committee approves a 6-month architecture sprint for the third chemistry (Months 30-36 = 2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14) while advancing the two confirmed chemistries into Month 36-84 (2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14) parallel-track optimization. T4 (USD 90 M) is released in full at Month 36 (2029-10-14) after selection-gate decision, preserving the USD 15 M pivot runway unused (stored as a strategic reserve for Year 5-7 extensions if needed). Monthly variance tracking ensures no surprise budget crises, and technology transfer planning begins in parallel with final optimization, enabling a timely delivery of verified 500 Wh/kg, 1000 Wh/L cells at Month 72 (2032-10-14) with clear licensing terms and manufacturer readiness by Month 84 (2033-10-14).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If detailed month-by-month cash-flow modeling cannot be completed by Month 1 (2026-11-14), adopt a quarterly cash-flow planning approach instead: develop detailed projections for Months 0-36 (2026-10-14 to 2029-10-14) in full, aggregate Months 36-84 (2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14) by half-year, and commit to a reforecasting review every quarter with updated monthly detail rolling forward 12 months (i.e., Month 6 = 2027-04-14 reforecast adds detail for Months 6-18 = 2027-04-14 to 2028-04-14).   • If reconciling the opex-versus-tranche gap (USD ~41 M shortfall Months 36-84 = 2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14) requires external co-funding or partner commitments not yet confirmed, defer detailed quantification of Months 36-84 (2029-10-14 to 2033-10-14) spending to the Month 24 (2028-10-14) T3 gate review: specify T3 gate conditions to include a completed refresh of post-Month 36 (2029-10-14) financial plan based on confirmed partner agreements and revised cost estimates, allowing the Steering Committee to adjust T4 allocation (USD 90 M total) at that point if needed.
  • If variance-tracking software or Finance Manager capacity is unavailable, establish a simplified weekly payroll and capital-spending dashboard (managed by Finance Manager or delegated to a 0.5 FTE Programme Finance Coordinator) tracking cumulative actual versus forecast for the current tranche only, with monthly escalation reports to the Steering Committee. This preserves early-warning capability without full monthly accounting overhead.
  • If decision-authority ambiguity persists, issue a Steering Committee charter document by Month 1 (2026-11-14) explicitly naming the authority responsible for each decision (e.g., 'Funder approves tranche release within 5 business days of Finance Manager gate-condition sign-off; Steering Committee Director certifies technical gate conditions met within 2 weeks of data submission').   • If contingency-drawdown mechanics cannot be fully specified by Month 1 (2026-11-14), issue interim emergency-spending authority (Steering Committee Director may approve <USD 500 K from the free contingency on an urgent basis, with retrospective Steering Committee review within 2 weeks; any draw >USD 500 K requires funder approval), and lock permanent drawdown rules into the locked funding schedule by Month 3 (2027-01-14).

Find Document 1: Lithium-Sulfur, Anode-Free and Conversion-Cathode Cell-Level Energy Density and Cycle-Life Data (2020-2026)

ID: 119d31a0-0e6d-4484-ad6e-09ff2dd3ec31

Description: Published or openly available data from peer-reviewed journals, national lab technical reports (NREL, ANL, PNNL Battery500 publications) and conference proceedings documenting measured cell-level (not material-level) Wh/kg and Wh/L for lithium-sulfur, anode-free lithium-metal, and conversion-cathode chemistries. Includes cycle-life degradation curves, thermal-runaway onset temperatures (differential scanning calorimetry and adiabatic calorimetry if available), and internal short-circuit failure modes. Intended audience: chemistry and materials teams for baseline performance understanding and identification of technological gaps relative to the programme targets (>=500 Wh/kg, >=1000 Wh/L, >=300 cycles).

Recency Requirement: Published within last 3 years (2023-2026 preferred; 2020-2026 acceptable for foundational results from Battery500 and related DOE programmes).

Responsible Role Type: Chemistry Pathway Lead with materials-science literature review support

Steps to Find:

  • Search Google Scholar, Scopus and Web of Science using keywords: 'lithium-sulfur cell energy density', 'anode-free lithium-metal pouch cell', 'conversion cathode cycle life', 'cell-level Wh/kg'. Filter for 2020-2026.
  • Download and review peer-reviewed journal articles (Journal of Power Sources, ACS Energy Letters, Nature Energy, Advanced Energy Materials) for cell-level data (not coin-cell or single-layer proxy numbers).
  • Access NREL, PNNL, Argonne and LBNL technical reports and annual reports from the DOE Vehicle Technologies Office and ARPA-E REFUEL programme (publicly available via www.osti.gov, ARPA-E website).
  • Contact Battery500 PNNL programme office (or equivalent DOE-funded consortia) to request published technical reports and benchmark pouch-cell data.
  • Compile a spreadsheet of measured cell-level Wh/kg, Wh/L, cycle count (to 80% retention), thermal-runaway onset by chemistry and development year.

Access Difficulty: Easy. Most DOE-funded Battery500 and NREL publications are freely available through OSTI.gov and journal open-access articles. Battery500.org website also hosts consortium publications and data summaries. Academic and national-lab preprints available via arXiv and ResearchGate. No authentication or fees required for government research data.

Essential Information:

  • Compile measured cell-level (not material-level) Wh/kg for lithium-sulfur, anode-free lithium-metal, and conversion-cathode cells from 2020–2026 peer-reviewed and DOE publications, with exact capacity ratings and current density to enable direct comparison with programme targets.
  • Quantify cycle-life data for each chemistry: number of cycles to 80% capacity retention (80% cutoff), degradation rate per 100 cycles, and variability across reported cells.
  • Identify thermal-runaway onset temperatures (differential scanning calorimetry or adiabatic calorimetry data) and internal short-circuit or dendrite failure modes for each chemistry class.
  • Capture volumetric energy density (Wh/L) from published pouch cells, including separator thickness, electrolyte volume and current-collector mass, to expose the volume/mass trade-off.
  • Establish baseline feasibility: can any reported cell simultaneously exceed 500 Wh/kg AND 1000 Wh/L? If not, identify the highest-performing published result for each metric separately and the penalty for dual achievement.
  • Document the technology gap: what interfacial, transport or mechanical barrier prevented published cells from reaching ≥300 cycles at ≥500 Wh/kg, and what the programme must solve.
  • List competing approaches within each chemistry class (e.g., ether vs. carbonate electrolyte for Li-S; oxide vs. halide separators for anode-free) and their respective energy-density and cycle-life trade-offs.
  • Provide author/institution context and funding source (DOE, ARPA-E, private) so the programme can identify potential academic or national-lab partners with relevant expertise.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Outdated or incomplete data (pre-2023 results, missing Wh/L numbers) allows the programme to build a chemistry strategy on superseded baselines, wasting 6–12 months discovering that an earlier published result already exceeded programme assumptions.
  • Material-level numbers presented as cell-level results inflate feasibility perception; the programme commits to a chemistry assuming 520 Wh/kg is achievable, only to discover at Month 30 (2029-04-14) that published pouch cells achieved 480 Wh/kg after packaging penalties.
  • Incomplete cycle-life data (only 100-cycle curves, no 300+ cycle data) prevents detection that a chemistry strategy reaches Wh/kg but fails the ≥300-cycle threshold; discovery at Month 36 (2029-10-14) gate forces a 6–12 month pivot.
  • Missing thermal-runaway onset temperatures or safety data lead to advancing a chemistry that later fails abuse testing, wasting 12–18 months of development and USD 10–20 M.
  • Absent author/institution metadata prevents identification of potential academic or national-lab partners, forcing the programme to reconstruct partnerships without background context on expertise and capability.
  • Incomplete volumetric-density reporting (energy per kg reported but not per litre) allows the programme to optimize only for gravimetric targets, discovering too late that 1000 Wh/L is unreachable with the chosen chemistry.

Worst Case Scenario: At Month 18 (2028-04-14), the chemistry tournament teams present projections based on incomplete or misinterpreted literature data. A lithium-sulfur candidate projected at 540 Wh/kg is selected as a finalist, but the underlying literature review missed competing publications showing dendrite growth below 200 cycles and volumetric collapse to 850 Wh/L. By Month 30 (2029-04-14), third-party pouch-cell verification reveals the candidate meets only 490 Wh/kg at 150 cycles and 820 Wh/L—failing both cycle-life and volumetric thresholds. The programme must pivot to a reserve chemistry at Month 36 (2029-10-14), but insufficient time remains for proof. Final result is a partial achievement (480 Wh/kg, 200 cycles, 850 Wh/L) that fails licensing appeal, or the programme misses the Month 84 (2033-10-14) delivery date entirely. Cost: USD 15–25 M wasted on a misdirected chemistry path, plus 12–18 month schedule slip and severely diminished invention value.

Best Case Scenario: The document provides a comprehensive 2023–2026 baseline showing that anode-free lithium-metal cells have achieved 520 Wh/kg at 280 cycles (falling short of 300), while lithium-sulfur cells achieve 510 Wh/kg at 150 cycles with severe volumetric penalties (800 Wh/L). Conversion-cathode work lags at 480 Wh/kg but shows 350-cycle potential. By Month 6 (2027-04-14), the chemistry teams identify the exact technical gap: anode-free requires interface engineering to extend from 280 to 300+ cycles (bridgeable in 12–18 months), and lithium-sulfur requires volumetric-architecture redesign. The programme deprioritizes conversion cathodes, focuses competing teams on anode-free versus Li-S with explicit interface and volumetric targets, and pre-stages a hybrid-electrolyte backup. At Month 30 (2029-04-14), a focused anode-free team delivers 505 Wh/kg, 320 cycles, 980 Wh/L, advancing to the Month 36 (2029-10-14) gate and leaving 48 months for refinement, safety hardening and technology transfer. Invention is credible, licensable and on schedule.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If published 2023–2026 cell-level data is incomplete or access-restricted, initiate targeted expert interviews (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) with Battery500 PNNL programme leads (contact via www.osti.gov or PNNL website) and NREL/Argonne electrochemistry groups to obtain unpublished technical reports, benchmark pouch-cell data and cycle-life curves by Month 6 (2027-04-14).
  • Engage the programme's selected university and national-laboratory partners (formalized by Month 3 = 2027-01-14) to conduct a critical literature review and synthesis of existing cell-level data, leveraging their institutional subscriptions and preprint access; complete by Month 9 (2027-07-14).
  • Commission a contracted technical literature analysis from a specialized firm (e.g., Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, IDTechEx, or academic consulting groups) to systematically extract and cross-validate cell-level Wh/kg, Wh/L and cycle-life data from 2020–2026 sources; budget USD 50–100 K and 6–8 week turnaround.
  • Build a live internal data-collection process (Month 4 = 2027-02-14): as the discovery teams build and test pouch cells, continuously populate a shared database with measured Wh/kg, Wh/L, cycle count and failure modes, establishing a contemporaneous internal baseline that is not dependent on external publication lag.
  • If a specific chemistry (e.g., anode-free solid-state) lacks sufficient published 2023–2026 cell-level data, contact the research groups directly (MIT, UC Berkeley, Carnegie Mellon) via Month 3 (2027-01-14) to request preprint or technical-report access before publication.

Find Document 2: Austin-Area Battery Technology and Electrochemistry Talent Market: Salary Benchmarks and Availability

ID: e14dec59-0022-46af-8231-b4af7bf46f6d

Description: Current (2026) salary survey data for battery scientists, electrochemists, materials engineers and manufacturing technicians in the Austin metropolitan area. Includes baseline and Tesla-proximity salary premium (proposed 15-20% estimate), benefits, and talent availability/turnover rates in the local battery and EV sectors. Intended audience: Talent Recruitment & Retention Manager and Finance Manager for payroll planning and recruitment strategy validation, addressing the USD ~4.8 M/yr payroll understatement risk flagged in pre-assessment.

Recency Requirement: Current as of 2026 (most recent available); 2025-2026 data preferred; 2024 data acceptable if 2026 is unavailable. Salary surveys from Glassdoor, LinkedIn, Mercer or battery-industry recruiters (Kforce, Allegis Group) are typical sources.

Responsible Role Type: Talent Recruitment & Retention Manager with Finance & Operations Manager

Steps to Find:

  • Contact battery-industry recruiters in Austin (Kforce, Allegis Group, Robert Half Technology) and request unpublished salary benchmark data or conduct a market survey of recent placements.
  • Search Glassdoor, LinkedIn Salary, Levels.fyi and Payscale using keywords: 'battery scientist Austin TX', 'electrochemist Tesla area', 'battery engineer Texas'; compile salary ranges and note any Tesla premium.
  • Request the 2025-2026 salary survey report from professional organizations (Electrochemical Society, American Chemical Society) if regional Austin data is included.
  • Contact UT Austin Office of Graduate Studies or McComb School of Engineering for guidance on postdoc and graduate-student salary benchmarks in Austin (lower cost, pipeline recruitment).
  • Reach out to established battery manufacturers or integrators based in or near Austin (e.g., Tesla Fremont HR benchmarking, or other EV suppliers recruiting in the area) for unofficial salary guidance (via confidential conversations with HR contacts).

Access Difficulty: Medium. Glassdoor and LinkedIn salary data are freely accessible but may be incomplete or aggregated nationally (requiring filtering for Austin). Professional recruiters and HR departments provide confidential data only upon request and relationship-building. Mercer and other major consulting firms' formal salary surveys are proprietary and require subscription or consulting engagement. Bottom-up estimate from 10-20 openly posted job descriptions (LinkedIn, company websites) plus informal recruiter conversations is a viable low-cost alternative.

Essential Information:

  • Establish current (2026) baseline salary ranges for key roles: battery scientist, electrochemist, materials engineer, manufacturing technician, and pilot-line engineer in the Austin metropolitan area, segregated by experience level (entry, mid-career, senior).
  • Quantify the Tesla-proximity premium (proposed 15–20% estimate) with empirical data from recent placements, LinkedIn salary reports or recruiter surveys, and validate against the programme's payroll budget of USD 10 M/yr baseline (estimated at-risk exposure: USD 4.8 M/yr shortfall if actual is USD 14.8 M/yr).
  • Document attrition and turnover rates for battery engineers in Austin (proposed risk threshold: >15%/yr), including data on poaching vectors (competing employers, salary drivers, non-salary factors such as prestige or equity).
  • Map talent availability and pipeline sources: postdoctoral and graduate-student salary scales at UT Austin and nearby institutions (propose 20–30% of team as lower-cost roles), tenure in role and cost-per-hire for each source.
  • Provide salary-adjustment recommendations tied to retention-risk thresholds: quantify the incremental cost (USD/yr) of a 15–20% senior premium, sign-on bonuses (USD 50–150 K range proposed) and professional-development budgets (USD 10–20 K/person/yr proposed) needed to compete with Tesla and other EV firms.
  • Compare Austin market data against national battery-industry baselines (e.g., Mercer, ACS/ECS salary surveys) to contextualize local competitiveness.
  • Document timing constraints: hiring for key chemistry and engineering leads must occur in Months 2–6 (2026-12-14 to 2027-04-14) to meet Month 18 (2028-04-14) discovery deadlines; identify which roles face longest lead times and require earliest recruitment.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Underestimated payroll costs: if baseline USD 10 M/yr assumption is incorrect and actual competitive compensation for 100 FTE reaches USD 14.8 M/yr, the programme faces a USD 4.8 M/yr shortfall (USD 34 M over 7 years), forcing either staff reductions, deprioritization of capital equipment, or underpaid hires of inferior technical depth.
  • Talent acquisition delays: without validated salary benchmarks by Month 2 (2026-12-14), recruitment offers may be non-competitive, causing hiring slips of 2–4 months for critical chemistry and engineering leads. Delays cascade to Month 18 (2028-04-14) discovery milestones.
  • High attrition and institutional knowledge loss: if compensation is insufficient and attrition exceeds 15%/yr, replacing 16–24 FTE annually consumes USD 1.5–2.5 M/yr in recruiting and onboarding, and loss of a key chemistry or characterization lead mid-programme (Months 12–24 = 2027-10-14 to 2028-10-14) sets progress back 2–4 months and USD 2–5 M.
  • Uncompetitive offers against Tesla and EV suppliers: absence of market data leaves the compensation strategy ungrounded; offers pitched below market risk losing candidates to competing employers, particularly for senior roles with longest lead times (3–6 months to hire).
  • Misaligned graduate and postdoctoral pipeline strategy: if UT Austin salary scales or availability are not confirmed by Month 1 (2026-11-14), the planned 20–30% lower-cost graduate roles may not materialize, invalidating the payroll-cost assumption and increasing average FTE cost by 5–10%.

Worst Case Scenario: If validated salary-market data is unavailable or substantially understates Austin's battery-talent costs (realistic risk given Tesla's proximity and recent EV sector hiring), the programme could face a cumulative payroll shortfall of USD 30–40 M over 7 years. Facing mid-programme payroll pressure (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-14 to 2028-10-14), the Steering Committee must either (1) cut staff from 100 FTE to 70–80 FTE, slowing discovery and jeopardizing chemistry-tournament completion by Month 36 (2029-10-14), or (2) raid the USD 20 M reserve to cover overruns, leaving no contingency for permitting delays, partner loss or chemistry pivots. Uncompetitive compensation combined with high attrition (20%+/yr) causes continuous re-hiring, loss of institutional knowledge, and inability to execute on characterization and cell-build cadence. Delivery at Month 84 (2033-10-14) could slip 6–12 months or the final cell result could be incomplete (e.g., 480 Wh/kg instead of 500, or missing abuse testing). Licensing credibility and patent value degrade if the cell is not fully verified and key personnel who originated the work have departed.

Best Case Scenario: Validated, granular salary-market data enables the programme to pitch competitive compensation offers (15–20% above baseline, sign-on bonuses USD 50–150 K, professional-development USD 10–20 K/person/yr) by Month 2 (2026-12-14), attracting and retaining key chemistry and engineering leads with <12% annual attrition. Confirmed UT Austin graduate and postdoctoral salary scales (USD 35–55 K/yr estimate) validate the 20–30% lower-cost-role strategy, keeping average payroll in the USD 9–11 M/yr range. Early hiring (Months 2–6 = 2026-12-14 to 2027-04-14) ensures full team capacity for Month 18 (2028-04-14) chemistry gateway, accelerating discovery loop and supporting a robust, reproducible pouch-cell build rate of 50–100 cells/month by Month 24 (2028-10-14). Predictable payroll costs free USD 2–5 M from contingency reserves for permitting, equipment or partner-access contingencies, improving overall programme resilience. Retention of key personnel through Year 3–4 ensures institutional continuity, publication credibility and a defensible, licensable patent estate by delivery at Month 84 (2033-10-14).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage battery-industry recruiters (Kforce, Allegis Group, Robert Half Technology) active in the Austin/Texas region by Month 1 (2026-11-14) to request confidential salary-benchmark data from recent placements (Dec 2025–Oct 2026); cost ~USD 2–5 K per inquiry or 10–15% placement fee for candidates, but provides real-time, unfiltered market intelligence.
  • Conduct a bottom-up salary survey by compiling 15–25 openly posted job descriptions from LinkedIn, company websites and ATS platforms (Tesla, NIO, other Austin EV/battery employers) and extracting salary ranges and requirements by role; cross-reference with Glassdoor, Levels.fyi and Payscale; aggregate across Months 1–2 (2026-11-14 to 2026-12-14), targeting 60–80% confidence interval rather than single-point estimates.
  • Request the 2025–2026 salary-survey report from professional organizations (Electrochemical Society, American Chemical Society, Materials Research Society) regional chapters; some publish regional salary data; cost typically USD 0.5–2 K for member access.
  • Contact the UT Austin Office of Graduate Studies, McComb School of Engineering and the Graduate School administrative team to obtain confidential postdoctoral and graduate-student salary and stipend benchmarks for Austin (lower-cost role strategy validation); cost zero; typically completed within 2 weeks.
  • Reach out to informal HR contacts at nearby established battery manufacturers or integrators (Tesla Fremont HR, Panasonic, Samsung SDI's North American operations, or local Tier-1 suppliers) via LinkedIn or conference networks and request confidential, off-the-record salary guidance; cost: networking investment (2–3 conversations per month over 2–3 months); outcome: directional data, not formal reports.
  • If formal market data remains unavailable by Month 2 (2026-12-14), assume worst-case payroll multiplier: use USD 14.8 M/yr (high-range estimate) instead of USD 10 M baseline in financial planning, allocate USD 50 M (17% of budget) to payroll instead of USD 70 M, and plan for 70–80 FTE at higher average cost; lock recruiting timeline to Months 1–4 (2026-11-14 to 2027-02-14) before budget pressure mounts.

Find Document 3: Austin Fire Authority and Texas TCEQ Hazardous-Materials Permitting Requirements and Timelines for Lithium-Metal and Solvent Research Facilities

ID: d434b270-5b22-4630-ba9c-bb11810bb337

Description: Current (2026) regulatory requirements, application templates, and typical approval timelines from the Austin Fire Authority, Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ), and Travis County Environmental Services for facilities handling lithium metal, organic solvents, and performing thermal-runaway and abuse testing. Includes Phase 1 (dry-room, inert-atmosphere glovebox operations), Phase 2 (reactive synthesis) and Phase 3 (abuse-testing chambers) permit scopes, conditional-use-authorization pathways to accelerate approvals, and hazardous-waste generator registration processes. Intended audience: EHS Officer and Programme Director for permitting-timeline and contingency-plan development, addressing the 6-8 month permitting-delay risk.

Recency Requirement: Current as of 2026; regulations typically stable but emergency rules or zoning changes can occur; 2024-2026 guidance documents preferred; 2020+ background acceptable.

Responsible Role Type: EHS Officer with Programme Director

Steps to Find:

  • Contact the Austin Fire Authority Marshall's Office (Fire Code and Permitting Division) directly by phone or email; request a pre-application consultation meeting (target within 7 days) and a written summary of permitting requirements for 'lithium-metal synthesis and thermal-runaway testing facility'.
  • Visit the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) website (www.tceq.texas.gov); download guidance on hazardous-waste generator registration (30 CFR 260-273 federal rules as adopted by Texas) and air-permit thresholds for volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions.
  • Contact Travis County Environmental Services and request zoning and facility-planning guidance for light industrial/lab use in Southeast Austin or Northeast Travis County (target locations per decision).
  • Search the Austin and Travis County municipal code databases (available online) for conditional-use-authorization procedures and expedited-permitting pathways for research facilities.
  • Request published timelines or case studies from TCEQ or fire authority on how long Phase 1 (dry-room only) and Phase 2 (synthesis) permits typically take (6-8 month estimate from pre-assessment; confirm or revise based on regulatory feedback).

Access Difficulty: Medium. Fire Authority and TCEQ staff provide guidance and published documents freely during pre-application meetings and via email. Published regulations (EPA and Texas codes) are free online. Zoning and conditional-use procedures are posted on municipal websites. However, specific timelines and internal approval processes are not always documented; direct contact with regulators and possibly a consultation with a permitting specialist or environmental attorney familiar with the Austin area may be needed to confirm realistic Phase 1 and Phase 2 approval schedules.

Essential Information:

  • Current (2026) regulatory requirements and application procedures from the Austin Fire Authority, Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ), and Travis County Environmental Services for facilities handling lithium metal, organic solvents, and performing thermal-runaway and abuse testing.
  • Phase 1 permit scope and timeline (dry-room, inert-atmosphere glovebox operations, anticipated approval window in days or weeks).
  • Phase 2 permit scope and timeline (reactive synthesis of lithium compounds, high-purity metal oxides, fluorinated solvents; approval window estimate, prerequisites for approval).
  • Phase 3 permit scope and timeline (abuse-testing chambers: thermal runaway, nail penetration, overcharge; approval window estimate).
  • Conditional-use-authorization pathways specific to research facilities in Southeast Austin or Northeast Travis County that accelerate approvals beyond standard timelines.
  • Hazardous-waste generator registration process (federal 40 CFR 260–273, as adopted by Texas) and annual reporting obligations.
  • Pre-application consultation procedures with Austin Fire Authority and TCEQ: contact methods, typical turnaround for preliminary guidance (target <7 days), what information to provide, and expected outputs.
  • Published timelines or case-study data from the Austin Fire Authority or TCEQ showing actual approval durations for similar facilities built in 2020–2026.
  • Permitted and prohibited materials or processes: which chemistries and work can proceed on-site and which must be outsourced to licensed facilities.
  • Conditional permits, phased approvals, or interim-operations authorizations that allow Phase 1 (dry-room only) to start while Phase 2 (synthesis) is pending.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Underestimated permitting timeline: if the document shows only a 4-week approval expectation and actual approval takes 6–8 months (as flagged in risk assessment), operational start slips from Month 3 (2027-01-14) to Month 9 (2027-07-14), compressing effective programme work from 81 to 75 months and forcing a months-long synthesis outsourcing at cost.
  • Incomplete Phase-1 versus Phase-2 separation: if permitting requirements are not clearly stratified, the programme may commit to a single monolithic permit application covering all three phases, delaying any operation (even dry-room work) until all phases are approved ~8 months later, instead of starting Phase 1 dry-room in Month 3 (2027-01-14).
  • Missing conditional-use pathways: if the document does not identify research-facility expediting or phased-approval procedures available in Southeast Austin or Travis County zoning, the programme defaults to standard industrial timelines, missing 2–4 month acceleration opportunities.
  • Absence of case-study timelines: without published data or regulator feedback on actual approval durations for similar facilities, the permitting schedule remains speculative; a programme built on a 3-month permitting assumption could face 8–12 month reality, cascading delays across hiring, equipment procurement and first pouch-cell builds.
  • Unclear materials restrictions: if the document does not specify which lithium-metal synthesis steps or solvents are permitted on-site versus must be outsourced, the programme either over-commits to on-site capabilities (and faces permit denial) or under-commits and incurs ongoing outsourcing cost (USD 2–5 M/yr estimate) without planning for it.
  • Missing prerequisites for Phase 2 approval: if conditional factors (proof of Phase 1 success, air-quality baseline data, staff training records) are not documented, the programme may not know what evidence to collect in Months 3–6 (2027-01-14 to 2027-04-14) to support Phase 2 (2027-04-14) application.
  • Regulatory change inattention: if the document is outdated (pre-2024) or does not flag recent rule changes (e.g., new EPA lithium-ion battery recycling or thermal-safety standards effective 2025–2026), the programme may design a facility and processes that become non-compliant mid-programme, triggering USD 2–5 M retrofits and operational shutdowns.

Worst Case Scenario: A permitting delay of 6–8 months (plausible given typical Austin Fire Authority and TCEQ workloads) prevents Phase 1 dry-room operations from beginning until Month 9 (2027-07-14) instead of Month 3 (2027-01-14), compressing the 84-month effective timeline to 75–78 months. Concurrently, unclear material-handling rules force conservation: lithium-metal synthesis is prohibited on-site, and the programme must outsource this critical step to a contract research organization (4–6 week turnaround, USD 50–100 K per batch, USD 2–5 M/yr estimate). This 18-month loss of on-site control and iteration speed delays identification of a viable chemistry by 6–12 months, pushing the Month 36 (2029-10-14) selection gate closer to Month 42–48 (2030-04-14 to 2030-08-14). With only 36–42 months remaining (instead of 48), final proof-of-concept and third-party verification of a 500 Wh/kg, 1000 Wh/L, 300-cycle cell may be incomplete or relegated to best-effort status, risking delivery of a partial or unverified result at Month 84 (2033-10-14). Programme credibility and licensing value suffer; technology transfer becomes uncertain. Alternatively, a serious incident (lithium-water fire, solvent spill) at Month 12–18 (2027-10-14 to 2028-04-14) due to misunderstood permitting or inadequate safety protocols triggers a 2–4 week facility closure, investigative delays and USD 1–3 M remediation, plus reputational and insurance damage, effectively ending the programme's timeline.

Best Case Scenario: A clear, current permitting document enables the EHS Officer and Programme Director to engage the Austin Fire Authority and TCEQ confidently by Month 0 (2026-10-14), with a pre-application consultation complete by Month 1 (2026-11-14). The document identifies a conditional-use-authorization pathway or research-facility expediting procedure that allows Phase 1 (dry-room and inert-atmosphere glovebox operations) to commence by Month 3 (2027-01-14) under an interim or phased permit while Phase 2 (synthesis) and Phase 3 (abuse testing) applications proceed in parallel. Clarity on which lithium-metal and solvent-synthesis steps are on-site permitted versus must be outsourced allows the programme to negotiate a hybrid model: Phase 1 and low-hazard synthesis on-site (reducing outsourcing cost to USD 500 K–1 M/yr for only the most aggressive precursor steps), and pilot-line commissioning on schedule by Month 3 (2027-01-14). First pouch-cell builds proceed in Month 6 (2027-04-14) as planned. Phase 2 approval arrives by Month 6 (2027-04-14), enabling on-site lithium-metal handling and synthesis by Month 9 (2027-07-14). Full in-house abuse-testing capability is operational by Month 12–18 (2027-10-14 to 2028-04-14). The programme executes chemistry evaluation and gate reviews on schedule, reaching the Month 36 (2029-10-14) selection gate with time and budget intact. Technology transfer and delivery proceed to Month 84 (2033-10-14) with no permitting-driven delays.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Initiate direct dialogue with the Austin Fire Authority Marshall's Office and TCEQ regional permitting offices in Month 0 (2026-10-14), before or alongside formal site selection, to obtain preliminary verbal guidance on timelines and material restrictions; document all guidance in writing (email summaries) to lock timelines and reduce uncertainty.
  • Engage a regulatory consulting firm or environmental attorney with Austin fire-code and TCEQ permitting experience (estimated cost USD 30–50 K for pre-application support) by Month 1 (2026-11-14) to accelerate permit pathway definition and identify conditional-use or expediting procedures specific to research facilities; use this as insurance against permitting-timeline surprises.
  • If Phase 1 permitting slips beyond Month 4 (2027-02-14), execute a contingency plan: lease temporary dry-room and basic glovebox space at an existing contract research facility or university lab for Months 4–9 (2027-02-14 to 2027-07-14) to begin initial synthesis work (e.g., coin-cell exploratory builds) while on-site facility is being permitted; estimated cost USD 50–100 K/month, budget USD 300–600 K.
  • Pre-negotiate a master service agreement with at least one Texas-based contract research organization (licensed for hazardous-materials synthesis) by Month 2 (2026-12-14) for outsourced lithium-metal and high-risk solvent work if on-site synthesis is prohibited or delayed; lock cost-plus pricing and turnaround terms (<4 weeks) in advance to mitigate operational delays.
  • Develop a phased on-site/off-site hybrid model documented by Month 3 (2027-01-14): design on-site work (dry-room assembly, lower-hazard characterization) to be Phase 1 permitted and executable by Month 3 (2027-01-14), and plan Phase 2 (higher-hazard synthesis) and Phase 3 (abuse testing) to be outsourced or deferred, allowing programme to start with a Phase 1 interim permit and avoid a 6–8 month monolithic approval.
  • If permitting delays extend beyond Month 6 (2027-04-14), initiate an early pivot to focus on chemistry and cell formats that can be developed and validated at partner university or national-laboratory facilities with existing permits (e.g., NREL, Lawrence Berkeley Lab partnerships); shift some in-house synthesis effort to partner labs, accepting longer turnaround (6–8 weeks instead of 1–2 weeks) but unblocking progress while Austin-site permitting continues.
  • Maintain a standing contingency funding reserve of USD 500 K–1 M for rapid re-permitting adjustments or facility modifications if regulatory changes occur mid-programme; allocate this within the USD 20 M general reserve to enable rapid response to new rules without budget re-cutting.
  • Establish a quarterly regulatory-monitoring subscription (estimated cost USD 10–20 K/yr) with a consulting firm to track changes in EPA, TCEQ or Austin Fire Authority regulations and alert the programme to required facility upgrades in advance, preventing mid-programme compliance surprises.

Find Document 4: Modular Dry-Room and Pouch-Cell Fabrication Equipment Vendors, Specifications and Lead-Times

ID: 61f0c338-1bf0-43a4-9b9c-537c4a2dfd3c

Description: Current vendor offerings and pricing for modular (containerized or relocatable) dry-room and pouch-cell fabrication systems (dew-point control <-30°C, electrode-coating uniformity ±10 µm, electrolyte-dosing precision ±2%, 50-100 cells/month capacity, estimate). Includes equipment specifications, lease vs. ownership terms, lead-times (order-to-delivery), and operating costs. Vendors: Mbraun (MOD drybox systems), Glove-box Company, or equivalent. Intended audience: Cell Engineering & Pilot-Line Manager and Finance Manager for pilot-line procurement and cost estimation, addressing the pilot-line capital-lock risk and operational-start timeline.

Recency Requirement: Current pricing and lead-times as of 2026 (as recent as possible; vendor quotes valid through Q1-Q2 2027 preferred).

Responsible Role Type: Cell Engineering & Pilot-Line Manager with Finance Manager

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Mbraun (Europe and US offices) directly via website (www.mbraun.com) or sales email; request an RFQ for modular dry-room and pouch-line package (50-100 cells/month, dew point <-30°C). Obtain lease and operating-cost terms.
  • Contact Glove-box Company (UK-based but supplies globally) and other dry-room system vendors (Phoenix Instrument, Inert Technology); request comparable RFQs.
  • Request references from existing users of modular dry-room systems (contact NREL, national labs, university battery centers) for feedback on lead-time accuracy and equipment reliability.
  • Search vendor catalogs and product datasheets (available on company websites) for specification verification (dew-point control range, coating-uniformity tolerance, electrolyte-dosing accuracy).
  • Request pricing for operating leases (cost per month, service included, exit terms) and capital-purchase options; clarify whether delivery is included in lead-time quoted or adds additional weeks.

Access Difficulty: Easy. Equipment vendors publish product specifications, lead-times and general pricing on their websites. Detailed pricing and custom lease terms require direct RFQ requests, but vendors respond within 2-4 weeks. References from existing users may require confidentiality agreements or can be obtained via academic/national-lab contacts. No special access or authentication required.

Essential Information:

  • Current vendor list and contact information for modular dry-room and pouch-cell fabrication systems capable of 50–100 cells/month production (estimate), including at minimum Mbraun MOD systems, Glove-box Company, Phoenix Instrument and Inert Technology offerings.
  • Detailed technical specifications for each vendor system: dew-point control range (<−30°C required), electrode-coating uniformity tolerance (±10 µm target), electrolyte-dosing precision (±2% target), cell-format compatibility (pouch preferred), and throughput capacity (cells/month).
  • Lead-time estimates (order date to full delivery and commissioning) for modular systems, with clarity on whether delivery time includes on-site setup and dry-room validation or adds additional weeks after equipment arrival.
  • Pricing: capital purchase cost (USD), operating-lease cost (USD/month, all-inclusive vs. service extra), service and maintenance terms, and residual value or buyout options at end of lease.
  • Comparison of lease versus capital-purchase financial terms: break-even analysis at 50, 75 and 100 cells/month throughput to inform the owned-versus-leased decision.
  • Vendor references from existing users (national labs, universities, contract research organizations) confirming lead-time accuracy, equipment reliability and actual operating costs.
  • Specifications for modular containerization: footprint, power and water requirements, ventilation and HVAC integration needs, and feasibility of relocating or expanding the system post-delivery.
  • Vendor standard warranty, performance guarantees, and spare-parts availability (lead-times for critical components such as dew-point sensors or electrode-coating heads).
  • Minimum order quantities and customization lead-time penalties if chemistry-driven specifications (e.g., ultra-precise electrolyte dosing for lithium-metal cells) differ from standard offerings.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate or outdated vendor lead-times (e.g., a vendor states 12 weeks but actual lead time is 6 months) delay site occupancy and first pouch-cell builds from Month 6 (2027-04-14) to Month 10–12 (2027-08-14 to 2027-10-14), compressing Month 18 (2028-04-14) chemistry gate by 4–6 months and reducing hypothesis throughput.
  • Missing or underestimated lease costs (e.g., service, maintenance, consumables) inflate annual pilot-line operational budget from USD 0.6–1.2 M/yr to USD 1.5–2.5 M/yr, consuming USD 6–10 M over 7 years and compressing characterization or partner budgets by 5–8%.
  • Specification gaps (e.g., dew-point control only to −25°C instead of −30°C, or coating uniformity ±15 µm instead of ±10 µm) necessitate process workarounds or equipment customization costing USD 1–3 M and adding 2–4 months to commissioning, delaying first reproducible cells to Month 8–12 (2027-06-14 to 2027-10-14).
  • Unverified vendor claims about modularity (e.g., system claimed relocatable but actually requires 2–3 month recommissioning and new permits if moved) trap the programme in a fixed location or add USD 3–5 M recapitalization cost if relocation becomes necessary.
  • Omitted customization penalties (e.g., a vendor quotes standard throughput 50 cells/month but the chemistry requires dual-temperature chambers, adding USD 2–5 M and 6–8 weeks to build) materially increase capital cost and delay commissioning.
  • Weak vendor financial stability or obsolescence risk (e.g., a quoted vendor exits the market or ceases production within 2–3 years) leaves the programme unable to procure spare parts or expand capacity, stranding the equipment.
  • No clear exit or buyout terms in lease agreements (e.g., end-of-lease obligation to remove equipment and restore facility at cost USD 500 K–1 M) hidden in fine print until Month 60–72 (2031-10-14 to 2032-10-14), creating surprise liabilities.
  • References from existing users not provided or outdated (e.g., references dated 2023–2024 on systems that have since been redesigned), leading to decisions based on obsolete performance or cost data.

Worst Case Scenario: Vendor information is incomplete, outdated or inaccurate: lead-times are underestimated by 6–12 months, technical specifications do not meet programme requirements (dew point, coating uniformity), customization costs exceed USD 3–5 M, or vendor financial instability means the equipment is unavailable when needed. Combined impact: pilot-line commissioning slips from Month 3–6 (2027-01-14 to 2027-04-14) to Month 9–15 (2027-07-14 to 2028-01-14). First reproducible pouch cells deliver to Month 12–18 (2027-10-14 to 2028-04-14), compressing the Month 18 (2028-04-14) gate and reducing early hypothesis throughput by 50%. Chemistry evaluation is delayed 6–12 months; a failing chemistry is not detected until Month 30–36 (2029-04-14 to 2029-10-14), eliminating runway for a pivot. Programme risks incomplete chemistry proof or forced descent to a lower-ambition result (480 Wh/kg instead of 500) by Month 84 (2033-10-14), or missing the delivery date entirely.
